title: Eva Marie Saint, "North by Northwest" star, dies at 102
summary: Eva Marie Saint won an Oscar for her film debut opposite Marlon Brando in "On the Waterfront." She bucked many Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career.
story: Academy Award-winning actor Eva Marie Saint, who starred in such classics as "On the Waterfront" and "North by Northwest," but also bucked Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career, has died. She was 102.
Her publicist, Jeff Sanderson, said she died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles, surrounded by family and loved ones.

A regal-looking blonde who ricocheted from playing sultry spies to Southern belles and Superman's stepmother, Saint made her motion picture debut opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's "On the Waterfront" (1954). Saint played Edie Doyle, whose brother was murdered by thugs working for a mob boss running a longshoremen's union; her character becomes involved with Brando's pugilistic dockworker Terry Malloy.

Her performance earned Saint one of the film's eight Academy Awards. (She was only the fourth person to win a best supporting actress Oscar for their film debut.) On the night she received her award, she was visibly pregnant. "I may have the baby right here!" she said. (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)

Saint married director-producer Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, and the couple stayed together for 65 years until his death in 2016. They had two children. Saint had made it clear that family was more important to her than her career.

"I had an agent once who wanted me to make many more movies," she told CBS' "Sunday Morning" in 2014. "I said, 'I can't. I can only do one a year, if that. I have children, young children.' And he said, 'Well, I guess you won't be a superstar.' And I said, 'Well, I guess not.'"
And what happened to that agent? "Fired him," she said.

She kept up her self-imposed limit on films; she also brought her extended family to the set of Otto Preminger's "Exodus" while filming in Cyprus and Israel. Despite not cranking out movies, Saint followed her Oscar win by appearing in many prestige projects, including "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "All Fall Down," "The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," and the eponymous TV miniseries based on "How the West Was Won." She also received five Emmy nominations, and won for the 1990 TV movie "People Like Us." At age 97, she appeared on a podcast series.

But perhaps her most memorable performance was as Eve Kendall, a mysterious blonde who crosses paths with Cary Grant's Roger Thornhill as he runs from murderous spies in the 1959 Alfred Hitchcock thriller "North by Northwest." Little does Thornhill realize that Kendall herself is a secret agent.
Saint said Hitchcock's direction to her playing a sexy spy was simple: "Three things: Lower your voice. Don't use your hands. And look directly into Cary Grant's eyes at all times," she recalled.

Hitchcock had a reputation for being tough on young female actors, but not Saint. "I found that he was such a wonderful director, gentleman, funny, courteous, but there are other actresses who don't feel the same way. I don't even want to hear stories about him," she said.
Though playing a femme fatale was new to her, Saint said she wasn't surprised upon watching her performance. "No. I don't think actors are surprised," she said. "I mean, that's what we do."
"Too innocent" looking

Born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, Saint grew up in upstate New York, and attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio (where she was "Sweater Queen"). Originally planning to become a teacher, Saint began acting in student productions, and changed her career focus.

Moving to New York City, she trained at the Actors Studio with famed acting coach Lee Strasberg, and was hired for a production of "Mister Roberts" alongside Henry Fonda. But she was let go by director Joshua Logan; she found out it was because she was deemed "too innocent" looking. The actor who took her place was Jocelyn Brando (Marlon's sister).
Crushed, she was nonetheless determined not to let it dissuade her from pursuing an acting career.

When she was starting out, she told Variety in 2021, Saint and a fellow female actor would talk in a made-up language while riding the subway. "We were so frustrated about not getting jobs, so I suggested that we do something so people would notice us," she said. "When we'd start gabbing, we'd get a little audience. People would put down their papers and wonder, what language is that?"

Saint established herself in the early days of live television as a dramatic actor in plays on "Studio One," "Goodyear Television Playhouse," "GE True Theater" and "Philco Television Playhouse." She starred in the first TV production of Horton Foote's "The Trip to Bountiful," and repeated her role on Broadway, where she was spotted by Kazan, the "Waterfront" director.

He asked Saint to audition opposite Brando in an improvised scene. Upon entering the room, Brando put on a radio, and the two started dancing. "He did something to flip my skirt, and I was so embarrassed I cried a little bit afterward," Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent in 2010. "But Kazan saw the chemistry, and he could see that it could work for the movie."
She said Brando was wonderful to work with.

"What was a little scary about him, which worked for me in the movie, was his perception of people that was so keen," she said. "He could look at somebody or talk with them and hone into what that person was all about. And he would mention it about people around us. So sometimes I would sit there and think, 'If he knows that about that person, he must know more about me than I know about myself.' It made me a little self-conscious, but I used that in the movie. He'd been out in the world and I had been at home protected, so I used that."
Following "Waterfont," Saint appeared on TV in a musical version of Thornton Wilder's "Our Town" with Paul Newman and Frank Sinatra, and also appeared onstage numerous theater productions.

But Hollywood beckoned, and the Oscar winner starred opposite such actors as Montgomery Clift and Elizabeth Taylor ("Raintree County"), Paul Newman ("Exodus"), Warren Beatty ("All Fall Down"), James Garner ("36 Hours"), Richard Burton and Taylor ("The Sandpiper"), Yves Montand ("Grand Prix"), Gregory Peck ("The Stalking Moon"), Bob Hope ("That Certain Feeling," "Cancel My Reservation"), and Tom Hanks ("Nothing in Common").
Other film credits included "Because of Winn-Dixie," "Don't Come Knocking" (with Sam Shepard), "Superman Returns" (as Martha Kent), and "Winter's Tale."

On TV she appeared in "The Best Little Girl in the World," "Moonlighting," the two-hander "Taxi!!" (opposite Martin Sheen), "The Last Days of Patton" (with George C. Scott), "I'll be Home for Christmas," "My Antonia," the 1996 TV miniseries "Titanic," and "Frasier."

And in recent years, Saint podcasted. She played Marisa Tomei's aunt in "The Bus Ride," a short play streamed on "The Pack Podcast." She said the feisty character, written by Eugene Pack, was compelling, calling his work "so honest."
"I've lived long enough to know what's honest and what isn't, and Eugene's plays are," she said. "They're charming, they're positive, but they're not saccharine."
Saint is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren and two great grandchildren, Sanderson's statement said.

title: Jim Bakker, who co-founded "The PTL Club" but fell into disgrace, dies at 86
summary: Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died at 86.
story: Branson, Mo. — Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show, "The Jim Bakker Show," there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.

"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," Lori Bakker said in a statement. "Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world."

But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, cultural icons - so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." A theatrical movie on their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021.

At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers' ministry included not only the TV show, which drew up to 13 million nightly viewers, but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.

They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show.
Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show.
In its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers - and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.

Sort of a Christian version of "The Tonight Show," it featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye - charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara - sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.
The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup.
Jim Bakker gets caught up in scandals

In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.
Things only got worse.

In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.
At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."

Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.
Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.
Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.

In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.
The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.
Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

title: Coco Gauff decries "insane" amount of online racism after China match dispute
summary: Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.
story: Beijing — Coco Gauff said she received an "insane" amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open match against home player Sun Xinran.

Gauff requested a video review, prompting some boos from the crowd, after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Sun, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title.

"Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said in a reply on X. "The amount of racist comments/dms I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."
Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing. The chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.
Gauff, a two-time Grand Slam champion ranked No. 4, went on to take control of the match on Monday.
"Xinran is (an) incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff added in another post.
Sun, who was given a wild card entry by tournament organizers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss.
Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledon as a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathized with Sun.

"I did not like to see her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career," Gauff said. "It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."

title: Aaron Sorkin on "The Social Reckoning": "Maybe we can't handle the truth"
summary: Sixteen years after "The Social Network," his Oscar-winning film about Mark Zuckerberg, Aaron Sorkin turns from Facebook's origins to its consequences with "The Social Reckoning," about a Facebook whistleblower.
story: Aaron Sorkin offered his remedy for writer's block: "I like to drive around and listen to music, and I try to start arguments with myself, talking out loud. … You're making me sound crazy now!"
But, he adds, that's where some of the best ideas come from. "One out of every 50 times, and I'll take those odds any day," he said.

The odds paid off when Sorkin was working on "The Social Network." Sorkin won an Oscar for screenwriting, and helped define Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg – and an entire industry – in the popular imagination.
Sixteen years later, Sorkin wonders about the unintended consequences.

"I remember talking to Jesse Eisenberg, who played Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Network,' and how distressed he was that teenage boys were coming up to him; they wanted him to sign business cards that said, 'I'm CEO, bitch,' the way Mark had it," said Sorkin. "Jesse was saying, 'Wait a second, these people think Mark is a hero in this story and not a tragic hero.'
"Of course, I'm responsible," Sorkin said. "It wasn't my intention."
And perhaps that's one reason why Sorkin is revisiting Facebook and Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning," out this Friday.

Jeremy Strong plays a grown-up Zuckerberg, still awkward but far more powerful. The film is inspired by the real-life story of Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (portrayed by Mikey Madison), who in 2021 leaked thousands of internal documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (played by Jeremy Allen White).
The Facebook Files (Wall Street Journal)
The Facebook Files (Wall Street Journal)

Haugen is still reflecting on Facebook, and Zuckerberg. "When I look at Mark, I view a lot of things about his experience of the world as a tragedy," she said. "Here's a person who rose to power when he was 19 years old, surrounded by yes-men for his entire adult life. He's been able to immediately isolate himself from consequences for 20 years."
The consequences for the rest of us are depicted in "The Social Reckoning": disinformation, extremism and division.

Sorkin says Facebook studied how and why its content was shared. "In 2018, engagement was going down, so they tweaked the algorithm," he said. "That is significant because they knew, they had done plenty of research showing that the things most likely to be reshared are anything that makes you angry – rage bait. That's what they did, and it worked."

On set in Vancouver this past July, we saw Sorkin (who's also directing the film) bring his signature rapid-fire dialogue to life. "I get very nervous when there aren't four walls," he said. "I've written very few exterior scenes in my life. It is mostly people talking in rooms."

Asked what he listens for when directing, Sorkin said, "Well, you used the word 'listen,' which is what I'm doing. I'm very conscious of the music of the language. My parents started taking me to see plays starting from when I was very little. And I loved the sound of dialogue. It sounded like music to me, just these great actors saying words that are crashing against each other. And I wanted to imitate that sound. And so, when I'm writing, what a line of dialogue sounds like is as important to me as what it means."

The movie opens just as Sorkin's first script, "A Few Good Men," returns to Broadway. Made into the 1992 hit film, it similarly examines another large institution wrestling with the truth. Its most famous line – "You can't handle the truth" – also seems to directly apply to "The Social Reckoning."

"I think the theme is you're not getting the truth in 'The Social Reckoning,'" said Sorkin. "I think that we can handle the truth, but ... you know what? I'm going to take that back. Maybe we can't handle the truth, and that the reason why so many people believe things that are flat-out untrue is that the lie is easier to believe.

"For instance, you can tell people 'til you're blue in the face that the undocumented immigrant population commits fewer crimes per capita than citizens; they won't hear that. They will only hear that immigrants are the cause of their problems," he said.
Meta, Facebook's parent company, declined to comment on the film. It's repeatedly said it's working to stop the spread of dangerous or harmful content.

The film arrives as Meta faces billions of dollars in settlements and verdicts over claims its platforms harmed the mental health of young users, with more cases headed to trial. And with Meta now competing in AI, whistleblower Frances Haugen worries. "There have been many whistleblowers that have come out of Meta's AI teams talking about the lack of safety," she said. "I would pause before rushing into giving Mark the level of power that he's trying to seize when it comes to AI."
It's the power Zuckerberg already wields that has kept Aaron Sorkin writing.

Asked what he would say to the Facebook co-founder if he had a moment with him face-to-face, Sorkin replied, "You want to make the world a better place? Don't make the truth up for grabs. Don't be indifferent to the truth. And he can do that."

title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner, Ken Urker, dies at 34
summary: Gypsy Rose Blanchard and Ken Urker connected while she was in prison for the 2015 murder of her mother, Clauddine "Dee Dee" Blanchard.
story: Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner, Ken Urker, has died at the age of 34, a Louisiana sheriff said.
An investigation into his death is underway. Capt. Brennan Matherne of the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office told CBS News that there are no signs of foul play. TMZ was first to report the news.

According to police records, Gypsy Rose Blanchard's half-brother and his wife, Dylan and Anita Blanchard, went to Urker's home and attempted to gain access to it. After failing to do so, Anita called the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office and requested a wellness check. She said that Urker was in a "dark place," owned a gun and had threatened suicide, according to the records. Officers were dispatched to the home around 6:15 p.m. on Thursday.

Anita told police that Dylan had knocked at the home's door for an hour with no response. Police said Dylan and another person, Justin Daigle, were eventually able to enter the home through an unlocked bedroom window. Daigle said that he touched Urker's body and realized he was cold and not breathing.

When police arrived on the scene, they found Urker dead in his bed. He "appeared to have been there for an extended period of time," police noted, with the report mentioning his face and arms had turned blue.
Next to Urker was a handgun, syringe and two shot glasses, according to the police report. Other drug paraphernalia, including a brown powdery substance, was found in Urker's bathroom, police said.
A cause of death has not been announced.
Thursday was Urker's 34th birthday.

Gypsy Rose Blanchard, 35, and Urker connected while she was in prison for the 2015 murder of her mother, Clauddine "Dee Dee" Blanchard. They share a 21-month-old daughter, Aurora. In a statement to People magazine, Gypsy Rose Blanchard said Urker's death was a shock.
"I'm in disbelief. I can't think," she said. "I've screamed until my throat burns."
"Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved," she told the outlet.
On Instagram, Blanchard wrote that Urker "will always be (her) greatest love story" and "will be remembered and loved forever."
Blanchard was previously engaged to Urker in 2018 and started dating him following her separation from ex-husband Ryan Anderson.

Blanchard and Anderson split up in early 2024, three months after they wed while she was in prison for her role in the murder of her mother. She had been sentenced to 10 years for second-degree murder over the death of her mother, who was killed by Blanchard's then-boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn. Blanchard, who accused her mother of subjecting her to years of medical child abuse, was released in 2023 after seven years in prison. Godejohn was sentenced to life in prison.

Anita Blanchard told the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office that Urker had recently made comments about being depressed and upset, and that he had not shown up to work on Thursday. Gypsy Rose Blanchard told People magazine that Urker "wasn't in a good state of mind lately" and had recently been a victim of cyberbullying.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard said on her Instagram story that the "cruelty directed toward" Urker "was something no human should have to endure."

"I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment," she wrote.
CBS News has reached out to Gypsy Rose Blanchard's rep for comment.

title: Anne Hathaway says she's learned to "chill out" in her career
summary: Anne Hathaway sat down with "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King to talk about her new movie, "Verity," what she's learned in her career and embracing her maternity style.
story: Anne Hathaway is reflecting on how she's changed throughout her career after a busy year starring in five films.

Hathaway told "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King she "had no idea" she would have five films debuting this year, adding she was worried it would be "a little bit" too much for people. Hathaway's latest film, "Verity," premieres on Friday.
"That's asking a lot of people to look at you for a long period of time, but then I thought to myself, 'What if it goes better than you can imagine?'" Hathaway said.
While looking back on her career, Hathaway said she's learned to "chill out" and is "more open to the fun of it."

"It's actually just about the feeling and the connection that you have with other people. And I wish that I had figured that out earlier in my life but I'm so grateful that I did at all," Hathaway said.
Embracing her maternity style
Anna Hathaway credited Rihanna for inspiring her maternity looks during her back-to-back press tours, saying the music star "changed the game."
"When I saw what she was doing with her maternity style, I just realized that I needed to use my imagination and go out there and have more fun," Hathaway said.
Hathaway said she's weeks away from welcoming her third child with husband Adam Shulman.

"We're thrilled. We're overjoyed. What we're really focused on right now is actually just taking in still being a family of four, because everything is going to change for us but it's really going to change for our kids. We're about to go through this beautiful threshold together," Hathaway said.
Her "creepy and eerie" role in "Verity"

Hathaway said collaboration was key when filming "Verity," a psychological thriller adapted from the bestselling novel by Colleen Hoover. Hathaway plays Verity Crawford, a renowned author who is incapacitated after an accident.

"When I knew my job was going to be very still in the frame and I wasn't going to have the ability to move around and act and work with the audience, collaboration became everything," she said, adding the small details in each scene became important.
Hathaway said they "jumped in with both feet and figured out how to make those shots creepy and eerie."

title: Congress tried to stop surprise medical bills. It created another problem.
summary: Healthcare providers and middlemen are exploiting a loophole in a 2020 law designed to shield consumers from surprise medical bills.
story: A law designed to protect patients from surprise medical bills succeeded in eliminating unexpected charges, but spawned a lucrative arbitration industry with providers and specialized middlemen extracting payments far above benchmark billing rates.
The practice is ultimately driving up healthcare costs for consumers, a CBS News investigation found.

The arbitration system Congress created to settle disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers allows doctors and resolution specialists acting on their behalf to win payments many times higher than typical rates for medical services. Those costs don't disappear: Much of the money comes from employer-sponsored health plans, meaning workers may ultimately pay through higher premiums or reduced benefits.

Under the arbitration system established by the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, insurers are paying healthcare providers hundreds of dollars for routine lab tests that typically cost between $10 and $30, industry researchers told CBS News. In one instance, a plastic surgeon was awarded more than $400,000 to perform a breast reduction, a procedure the insurer said it had previously paid the doctor between $6,000 and $30,000 to perform.
The plastic surgeon, Dr. Norman Rowe, routinely was awarded around 170 times the benchmark rates for his services under the NSA's arbitration system, a CBS News analysis of public data shows.
A spokesman for Dr. Rowe told CBS News that insurers had manipulated benchmark rates to lowball doctors and create "artificially low reimbursement rates."

"Dr. Rowe uses the widely recognized gold standard FairHealth benchmarks set by the independent nonprofit FairHealth.org using reliable and objective market data. FairHealth data is so reliable that it is incorporated into statutes and regulations around the country and serves as the official data source for many state health programs," the spokesman added.

In addition to the typical benchmark rate arbitrators consider (known as the "qualifying payment amount," or QPA), FairHealth provides another rate that can be used during the dispute resolution process. Medicare rates, meanwhile, may not be considered.

CBS News found that another doctor — Long Island spine surgeon Vadim Lerman — was being awarded an average of 280 times the benchmark rates in arbitration. He declined an interview, but a spokesman for Lerman said that "the suggestion that a physician is receiving 'hundreds of times' above benchmark rates is incorrect. No comparison should be made to the insurer's initial offer — which can be inappropriately low for a complex surgical procedure — and the award given to the physician."
"Baseball-style arbitration"
Insurers have, in many cases, been forced to pay high rates like those Dr. Rowe charges under the law's so-called "baseball-style" or "pendulum" arbitration system.

In an arbitration under the No Surprises Act, insurers and providers each propose a rate for a given service. There's no room for negotiation, as an arbitrator must choose between one of the two parties' suggested figures.

Arbitrators side with providers in more than 85% of the cases, according to Leland Robbins, a product leader at Turquoise Health, a data transparency startup. Some arbitrators – officially called certified Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR, entities – have track records of siding with providers in an even larger share of cases, according to Robbins' group.
He told CBS News that while patients are no longer being surprised by large medical bills, there is a catch to the new system.

"The transaction didn't go away. It went behind closed doors and has moved into this arbitration process when a payer and a provider can't agree what the fair price should be," Robbins said. "Given that 70% of these awards are being taken out of employer-sponsored health plans, consumers are going to start seeing it when it comes time for open enrollment."
He added, "You know, employers are not able to withstand and absorb these kinds of big fees. They're going to be probably not paying for as much of your premiums."

Last year, 15 government-certified arbitrators earned fees per case, with 17 arbitrators designated to do this work today. Each side in the dispute — the healthcare provider and the insurer — pays into the process prior to the arbitrator making any decision.

During the first six months of 2025, insurers and providers submitted 1.2 million new disputes to the arbitration portal, while federal officials had only expected approximately 17,000 cases per year, research from the Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR) at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy shows.
However, HaloMD, a company that files cases on behalf of providers, told CBS News that the initial estimates "were objectively flawed in how they calculated expected volume."
Collectively, arbitrators making the decisions have earned more than $2 billion in fees. None agreed to on-camera interviews with CBS News.
New Jersey House Rep. Frank Pallone, a Democrat and the lead sponsor of the No Surprises Act, blames private equity, in part, for breaking the system he helped create.
He said just a few private equity firms – which are increasingly buying up anesthesiology, radiology and emergency room practices — are driving arbitration cases.

Pallone told CBS News that doctors should be paid the equivalent of in-network rates for the services they provide, but said "we had no choice" but to introduce the arbitration system "if we wanted to actually get rid of surprise billing."
"I knew it was not going to go well, but I didn't know it was going to be this bad," he added.
Dispute resolution cottage industry

The law's arbitration provision has also created an opportunity for intermediaries to guide providers through the process and rake in profits by taking a cut of bills that are up to 1,000% above the benchmark rate for a service, CBS News found. Critics argue that such firms demand more money on providers' behalf, leading to the large settlements that drive up everyone's costs.

HaloMD bills itself as "the expert" in arbitration cases brought under the No Surprises Act. Founded by Texas couple Scott and Alla Laroque in 2022, the same year the No Surprises Act took effect, the company is one of the fledgling industry's biggest players.

Private equity firms also sometimes own both physician staffing firms and Independent Dispute Resolution entities, creating a conflict of interest and undermining the law's fairness. HaloMD is not private equity-backed, but Halo and two other groups with investments from buyout firms collectively handled more than 75% of disputes settled in arbitration last year, according to Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms.

According to Halo, the firm made more than $1 billion for its clients, routinely earning awards that are nine times the benchmark rates for services. Halo takes a cut of the payouts but has not disclosed the amount.

Halo chief external affairs officer Patrick Velliky told CBS News that insurance companies, not firms like his, are responsible for driving up consumer healthcare costs by either not participating in the arbitration process or submitting ludicrously low offers.

"24% of the time, insurers lose by default. They didn't submit an offer at all. Another 9 1/2% of the time, insurers submit an offer, like a dollar or less," Velliky told CBS News. "So what that actually looks like, a patient goes to the E-D with a heart attack, we go to arbitration and the insurer is offering a total of $1.00."

He also said that insurance companies are offering misleading information about the benchmark rate. "Whatever the actual median in-network rate is, it's not what the insurer presented," Velliky told CBS News. "They're miscalculating it."
A federal court sided with providers on the issue this summer, saying the benchmark rate is "artificially low," pulled down by insurers' $0- or $ 1-reimbursement offers to doctors.
Proposed reforms
Pallone wants to reform the law to gut what he sees as the root of the issues arising from the No Surprises Act: arbitration.

He plans to introduce legislation this week to eliminate the arbitration process and stipulate that providers be paid in-network rates, even if they are out-of-network. Pallone's office also told CBS News that so-called ghost rates, which often drag the benchmark rate down, will be excluded from calculations moving forward.

"Whether it's the hospitals, the doctors, the nurse, they're really trying to care for people. Of course, all of them should have a decent income so they can live," the New Jersey lawmaker said. "But why should these outside investors be making all this money off the backs of, you know, your insurance premiums, essentially?"

title: Rubio calls on Russia to be more open about plague lab worker's death
summary: The World Health Organization says public risks are low after a plague center worker's death, but Marco Rubio says Moscow should "share more information with the world."
story: Geneva — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia to be more "transparent" about the recent death of a plague research center scientist and any risks associated with the incident, which Russian authorities have offered conflicting information about this week.

"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio said Tuesday after arriving in Iceland's capital Reykjavik for a visit. He called on Moscow to be "transparent" a day after Russia's primary national health agency denied earlier reports by local officials that the Siberian lab worker might have died of plague after a lab accident and that anti-plague measures were imposed at multiple health facilities in the wake of her death on Oct. 1 or 2.
The World Health Organization said Tuesday that the public health risk in Russia and Europe was considered low after the incident in Russia's far-eastern Siberia region.

"The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region," the United Nations health agency's spokesman Christian Lindmeier told reporters at the agency's Geneva headquarters.

Lindmeier said Russian authorities had identified all people who came into contact with the worker from the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, who has been identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, before she died and that none had symptoms associated with plague.
The center where Shipilova worked is situated in a part of Siberia where plague is found naturally in wild animal populations, the WHO spokesman confirmed.
Lindmeier said her "illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection," but that Russian authorities "are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death."
"WHO is following the situation closely, working with headquarters to keep other countries informed," he said, and is ready to help Russian authorities if they seek assistance.

Russia's national health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, played down reports Monday by some officials in the Siberian region —   some of which were quickly removed from online platforms — indicating that Shipilova had died after contracting plague in a lab accident.
The agency said she was not diagnosed with plague, but died of "pneumonia of unknown etiology," suggesting doctors didn't know the exact germ that made her sick.

She died in an Irkutsk hospital two days after contracting the illness. The hospital where she was treated, and where her roughly 200 close recent contacts were evaluated, was then partially shut down under quarantine conditions, Russian authorities said. They rejected reports that several other health facilities in the region were also put under restrictions as a precaution.
Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that an analysis of samples from Shipilova revealed no microorganisms associated with her work, which involved handling dangerous pathogens at the lab.

The agency said Tuesday that many of her close contacts, having been brought in for screening, were allowed to go back home. It said some cold and flu infections, including several COVID-19 cases, were discovered, but nothing more sinister.
President Trump assured reporters on Monday that U.S. officials were watching the case closely and stood ready to help.

"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," he said. "They call it pneumonia, and pneumonia, you know, years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger disproportionately. But we'll help them."

title: Russia plays down reported plague lab death and says, trust us
summary: A Russian plague lab worker died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," officials say, in response to initial reports that she was exposed to the deadly bacteria during a lab accident.
story: Russia's government played down concerns Monday sparked by media reports that a female scientist in Siberia might have died of exposure to the plague after a lab accident.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that the state health watchdog known as Rospotrebnadzor was the "lead agency with expertise in this area," and he urged Russians to "listen to official information" from its "highly qualified professionals."
The researcher who died has been identified by Russian reports as Darya Shipilova, 28, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute more than 2,500 miles east of Moscow.
Russian media initially reported that she broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and then died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said she died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.

The plague bacterium referred to by the reports is yersinia pestis, the same one that caused the Black Death that swept across Europe in the mid-1300s, killing an estimated 25 million to 50 million people. That pandemic, often referred to as the bubonic plague, was spread by fleas living on rodents and other animals in close proximity to — and in the same grim sanitary conditions as — people.
The pathogen, if untreated, can cause swelling, fever and death.

Shipilova, according to Russian media, died from the pneumonic plague, which is caused by the same bacteria but attacks the lungs and causes a fever and a cough that can turn bloody. Pneumonic plague can be transmitted from person to person, unlike bubonic plague, and can also be fatal.

The head of Russia's eastern Republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, initially said Shipilova died of the plague in a post on the state-backed messaging app MAX. He later edited the post to add the word "possibly," according to an independent regional Russian media outlet that operates in exile, Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal).
He was not the only Russian official to walk back their words on the story.
Local officials initially warned people not to visit the town of Shelekhov, where the scientist was hospitalized and later died, citing "unofficial information" about a human plague case.
The post was deleted less than two hours later, according to both Lyudi Baikala and Astra, another independent news website.
Since then, Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has said it carried out "anti-epidemic measures" that included testing nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova.

The agency said some people had tested positive for colds or COVID, but that no pathogens causing dangerous infections were found. It also said there had been no accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and it attributed the scientist's death to "pneumonia of unknown origin."
A WHO spokesperson said that based on the unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general public appears to be low.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the reports of a suspected plague case in Russia were not cause for alarm, but "for focus."

"We know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided," he said. "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread."

But Rubio said, given "very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia," he did not believe it was "cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus, and a cause to just keep an eye on it, and we're doing that."

title: Alan Alda on fighting Parkinson's with laughter
summary: Alan Alda, now 90, best-known for his role as "Hawkeye" Pierce on the classic TV series "M*A*S*H," talks about living with Parkinson's disease, which he refuses to let define him.
story: Is it even possible to choose a favorite Alan Alda character? How about Senator Arnold Vinick on "The West Wing"? Or lawyer Jack Burroughs in "The Four Seasons"? And, of course, "Hawkeye" Pierce, the sarcastic Korean War combat surgeon, on "M*A*S*H"?
For his work on "M*A*S*H," which aired on CBS for 11 seasons beginning in 1972, Alda won five of his six Emmy Awards for acting, writing and directing.

"I have doctors coming up to me on the street all the time telling me that seeing me in the show made them want to become a doctor," Alda said. "Not a single one said it made them want to become an actor!"

Long before playing Pierce, Alda – now 90 – was on the other side of the stethoscope. As a seven-year-old he had polio, before there was a vaccine. "My father had just gotten a huge part in a movie, playing George Gershwin," he said. "And about a week after he started shooting, I got polio. And he and my mother had to administer the treatment, which was almost-scalding hot packs of wool on every limb. So, they were practically torturing their kid. I remember thinking it was hard on them."

As a boy, Alda studied his father Robert Alda's performances in vaudeville and burlesque, and also on Broadway, when Robert starred in the original cast of "Guys and Dolls." "I stood in the wings and watched that every Saturday," Alan said.

But Lady Luck dealt the family a difficult hand. His mother, Joan, a former beauty pageant winner, was complicated. "My mother was mentally ill, had schizophrenia and was paranoid," Alda said. "So sometimes the communication would be about the crack in the wall was where they had a camera taking pictures of us. I think that contributed a lot to tools I later had, trying to figure out what's real and what's not real. I had to pick one reality and try to stick with that. … It made me more observant. And I think it even helped – I'm just realizing this for the first time in this moment! – I think it made me a little more curious."

He's been especially curious about human connection, something he fostered on the set of "M*A*S*H." "We didn't go back to our dressing rooms between shots," he said. "It was just, like, an hour or two hours where they light the new set, we stayed in our chairs in a circle and made fun of one another and laughed. And that connection that we had, we carried with us onto the set."
Which had a huge impact on viewers. More than 100 million people watched the series' final episode. "They think 106. But I think it was probably more. Not that I'm greedy!" he laughed.

For years, Alda has been concerned that scientists and health care professionals often use technical language that's hard for the general public to understand. With that in mind, in 2009, New York's Stony Brook University founded the Alan Alda Center for Communicating Science. Back in 2013, our own Tracy Smith watched Alda use methods from his own acting experience, including improvisation.
He said, "Improvisation really puts you in touch with the other person, and that's when I realized the value of connection."
Connecting is one of Alan Alda's superpowers. Since 2018, on his podcast "Clear+Vivid," he's been interviewing guests like Paul McCartney, Michael J. Fox, Noah Wyle, and recently, Joy Behar.

To Alda, connecting with people means being clear and honest, which is why he will openly discuss his Parkinson's disease. "I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."
At the time he had no other symptoms: "I had no twitch, no tremor, no problems with my voice."

He was 79. A few years later, Alda decided to reveal the diagnosis. "I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."
There's currently no cure for the neurological disorder, but there are medications and other treatments. "I don't let Parkinson's define me," he said. "It's not who I am. It's just a hobby."

Which brings us to what Alda considers the importance of a sense of humor: "Very important, because the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

But what is funny about Parkinson's? "I'll be at the computer keyboard writing an email, and Dr. Parkinson is moving my hand all over the screen. I have the mouse, and he's eliminating things and he's deleting things that I need," Alda laughed. "Once in a while I get frustrated. But I find what makes me laugh about it, and then I go tell Arlene. Laughing first brought us together. We were invited to dinner at a friend's house. And Arlene was sitting at one end of the table, and I was sitting at the other end. And I noticed that she was laughing at my jokes. So already I was smitten. In March, we'll be married 70 years."
They have three daughters and eight grandchildren.

Alan Alda says he feels really good, even if Arlene has to help button his shirt in the morning, which he admitted he hated. "Of course, I feel that from time to time," Alda said. "I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: what haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"

title: Book excerpt: "Narratives" by Nancy Colier
summary: In her latest book, the psychotherapist writes about how the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves can hold us back from living a more truthful and connected life.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

In her latest book, "Narratives: Let Go of the Stories That Keep You Stuck" (to be published Nov. 3 by New Harbinger Publications), psychotherapist Nancy Colier writes about how the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves can hold us back from living a more truthful and connected life.
Read the excerpt below, and don't miss Susan Spencer's interview with Nancy Colier on "CBS Sunday Morning" Oct. 4!

Legend has it that Harry Houdini failed at only one publicly performed escape attempt. As the story goes, Houdini accepted an invitation to escape a maximum-security jail cell, in order to display and prove his skills. But despite working all his lock-picking magic for hours, he simply couldn't get it to open. Defeated and exhausted, he collapsed against the cell door only to discover that it swung open on its own. Turns out, it was never locked in the first place. The only place the door was locked was inside his mind; he was a prisoner only in his story of imprisonment.
All too often it's not life that imprisons us, but the stories we tell ourselves—about our life. The narratives inside our heads are the real obstacles to freedom and happiness.
And so begins our story…

My friend Francesca was incensed. She'd been invited to be a bridesmaid at her friend's destination wedding in the Bahamas. In the story she told me, the bride had only asked her to be a bridesmaid because she assumed that Francesca would never get married herself. And, because she couldn't possibly have other plans and therefore could just slip off for a four-day trip to the Bahamas at the drop of a hat—with only nine months' notice! In my friend's narrative, the invitation to be a bridesmaid in the Bahamas was insulting and humiliating; the bride obviously thought she was pathetic, and was "throwing her a bone."

A few days later, I was eavesdropping at my local diner—my favorite laboratory for human behavior. At the next table, a couple in their midforties were chatting about a movie they'd just seen. As the waiter zoomed by without stopping, the man became visibly agitated. I heard him tell his partner that it was the third time the waiter had "ignored" him and that if he were "a somebody who people respected," then they would already be enjoying their burgers. When the server finally did arrive, sweat bubbling above his lip, I heard this man aggressively asserting that the young man should be less obvious about whom he deems important enough to serve. My dining neighbor was just a normal person doing what normal people do, creating a story and crafting meaning. But the particular meaning we make—the specific story we tell ourselves—this is our personal narrative and, more than anything else, what determines our reality. Just this morning, I was late to meet a colleague because I unexpectedly had to take my daughter to the doctor. Not long into our meeting, my colleague made a comment about not being able to rely on anyone and always having to take care of herself. When I asked her what she meant by that, she brought up the fact that I'd been late despite our having twice confirmed the time. I had been late, that part was true, but she'd also never asked why or inquired about what happened on my end. And ironically, she'd told me many times that I was someone she could count on, and how much she appreciated that aspect of our relationship. In the nine minutes she'd been waiting for me to arrive that day, she'd written a comprehensive story that used my tardiness as an endorsement for her preexisting narrative. Needless to say, this compelled me to get home and keep writing this book.
One World … Billions of Universes

Everyone we know (including ourselves) is walking around with a personal movie playing inside their head—a movie they're fully absorbed in and believe is real. If that weren't strange enough, we're also all assuming that our movie is the same movie everyone else is watching, and the only one showing. In a nutshell, our movie is reality. Unfortunately, we're all thinking the same thing.

Usually, the only thing that's the same in all our movies is the person playing the main character. The star of the story is our self—the me character. How is this experience for me? Do I like it or not? Does it bring me pleasure or pain, serve me or harm me? Boiled down, this is what we want to know. Our narrator writes her story from a first-person POV and creates a world in which everything reflects, relates to, and, ultimately, is about us. Not because we're all raging narcissists, but because under our stories lies a basic drive to do two things: create meaning and survive. Our stories, in one way or another, are always trying to make it possible for us to survive as a distinct and identifiable self.

From the cradle to the grave, we're weaving our perceptions into a cohesive personal storyline. We create a plotline that makes sense of reality and makes the world feel knowable. Our stories help us create a consistent and cohesive self, which we need to function in the world.

Problems arise because we don't realize we're watching a personal movie inside a personal cinema, a movie that no one else is watching. We become the character in the movie and imagine that everyone else is also the character we've scripted them to be. We then respond and react with this assumption, believing that others are operating with the intentions and emotions we've designed for them. The movie playing in our head is not our reality, it's the reality; it's not just what we're seeing, it's what is. And yet, in actual reality, what we've deemed reality is just a bundle of interpretations created by a biased narrator and run through a highly curated lens, shaped by a unique and personal history and edited to fit into our already existing sense of self.

We don't just believe our story, however; we also will do whatever it takes to defend it … no matter what the cost is. Have you ever noticed that the stories you tell yourself often don't support or encourage you, help your relationships, or make you happier? And in fact they often make you unhappier? And yet, you hold on to them.  Even when the facts directly contradict your story, you can't be dissuaded from its beliefs. Your loyalty is to your story—not your happiness.
From "Narratives: Let Go of the Stories That Keep You Stuck" by Nancy Colier, published by New Harbinger Publications. Copyright © 2026 by Nancy Colier. Reprinted by permission of the author.

title: Letting go: Why holding onto grudges can be damaging
summary: Studies show people who hold grudges have greater levels of cardiovascular trouble, and higher levels of depression and anxiety. Experts say those taking steps towards forgiveness can have better outcomes.
story: Journalist Meredith Lepore admits it: She really can hold a grudge. She says her typical grudge can last five to seven years – or even longer! She felt snubbed when 12 years ago friends didn't give her a bigger role in organizing a bachelorette party.
"I don't think I ever planned a bachelorette party after that," Lepore said. "There was too many cooks in the kitchen, and I didn't like that."

In her twenties, she took offense when a roommate yelled at her for locking herself out of their apartment. Is she still made at her? "I would have a drink with her, but I would never call her a friend," Lepore said.

But the granddaddy of her many grudges centers around – of all things – a birthday cake back in college: "My parents had sent me a birthday cake. So, I put the birthday cake in the fridge one night, and then the next morning it was gone. Somehow we figured out that a boy had taken it late at night – he was, like, telling people about it, and, like, boasting about it."
Asked if she's still mad about that ("It was a nice cake!"), Lepore replied, "I've held that one for a long time. I think now I'm over it!"

Lepore says she comes by her grudge-holding honestly. "My father – nicest guy, a brilliant doctor, you know, kindest bedside manner – we've always joked that he was gonna write a book called 'Grudges I've Had,' you know, just about lifelong grudges."
So, it runs in the family? "Yeah. I think it does," Lepore said.

Asked about other traits that she thinks leads her to become more inclined to grudges, Lepore replied, "I am a sensitive person. I think some people are much better at letting things roll off their shoulders."
"It's very childlike"
Grudges are incredibly common, with one survey finding four out of five adults (78%) harbor some lingering resentment, with the average holding seven grudges at the same time.

Psychotherapist Nancy Colier (author of the upcoming book "Narratives: Let Go of the Stories That Keep You Stuck") says, in her practice, she sees patients holding grudges every day. "It is absolutely remarkable to me how small, small events can become just enormous, poisonous hives inside of someone," she said.

And those hives, says Colier, can buzz for decades: "I am working with one person who is holding on to a grudge against a high school friend – this a person in her fifties – over a scuffle to do with a boy when they were 17. She's still furious, still walking around angry."

But all of this is counterproductive. "We're lighting ourselves on fire, and expecting the other person to die of smoke inhalation," Colier said. "We have this misguided idea that we're punishing the other person."
According to Harvard epidemiology professor Tyler VanderWeele, "Unforgiveness is essentially like drinking a poison and hoping the other person dies. It doesn't work."
VanderWeele says, whether held for a day or a decade, grudges are just bad for us: "Studies indicate greater levels of cardiovascular trouble, higher levels of depression, higher levels anxiety."

Yet, we live in an age where brazen airing of a grudge, once frowned upon, now seems almost expected. "There are multiple reasons for this change," VanderWeele said. "One of them is the public nature of the grudges that are now possible through social media. Some of it also is an abandonment of discussions of character and what good character looks like and what good character requires."
It also seems to be in fashion politically, with politicians now wearing their grudges on their sleeves. According to Colier, "It's very childlike."
So, how to rid yourself of a grudge? At Harvard's Institute of Human Flourishing, Vanderweele focuses on one word: forgive.

"Forgiveness is the letting-go of a grudge, the replacing of ill will towards an offender with goodwill," he said. "It's not all that needs to take place to provide restoration and reconciliation, but I do think it's always appropriate. Have goodwill, even when one's been hurt."
"Anger becomes like a sickness"

Author Immaculée Ilibagiza is living proof of the incredible power of forgiveness. She lost most of her family to the Rwandan genocide. Ilibagiza survived by hiding in a tiny bathroom with seven other women for three months.
Asked what that experience did to her spirit, Ilibagiza replied, "My goodness, I was fighting with God. I was asking him questions. I was angry."

But somehow, she learned to let go of that rage when she realized it was harming only her. According to Ilibagiza, when you are angry you are married to your enemies. "Anger becomes like a sickness. It becomes like an obsession," she said.

Today, Ilibagiza, whose experience might justify holding a grudge against all of humanity, instead tours the world preaching forgiveness. VanderWeele said, "Examples like that are incredibly profound, and I think demonstrate the power and the freedom that forgiveness can bring."

So, Nancy Colier says, we must deal with all grudges – whether large-scale like Rwanda, or mundane as a birthday cake – the same way: "Ultimately, your well-being cannot rely on anyone else changing, or doing anything for you. It cannot, or we're hostage. The only way you're going to feel well, find equanimity, is when you take ownership of your own well-being. Get them out of your story."

title: "America's Startup" competitors use AI to launch businesses from their dorms
summary: Young entrepreneurs are tapping AI to launch a range of businesses, from analyzing your skin to helping wine growers analyze crop yields.
story: One startup uses artificial intelligence to help winemakers better predict crop yields. Another uses insights gleaned from AI to enable earlier detection of skin cancer, while a third develops a seaweed-based hydrogel fire suppressant that's free of "forever chemicals."

The entrepreneurs behind these tech-forward startups have one thing in common: They started the companies from their college dorm rooms to participate in "America's Startup," a government-backed collegiate innovation competition that's part of America250, the congressional commission behind the U.S.'s 250th anniversary celebration.

America250 chair and the 43rd Treasurer of the U.S., Rosie Rios, who leads America's Startup, told CBS News she expects a wave of innovation led by Generation Z entrepreneurs, who will be the first AI-native cohort of workers to enter the job market upon graduation.

"They really hit the ground running and are not intimidated by it," Rios said. She also thinks AI will help broaden the skills and experience of new entrants to the job market, much as the internet did for millennials.
"It's no longer what they learned at home or in a classroom — it's what they see and have access to," said Rios, adding that AI helps eliminate some of the hurdles to launching companies.
"Idea machines"

Recent research from the Bank of America Institute shows the rate of U.S. business formation is rising, largely driven by Gen Z founders. In June, Gen Z surpassed all other generations in growth in new business registration applications. Researchers concluded that starting a business may be viewed as a desirable pathway to career success as younger workers navigate a challenging labor market.

Additionally, AI can be deployed to perform functions such as bookkeeping or content creation, allowing founders to operate as "solopreneurs" and save on personnel costs, researchers at the Bank of America Institute noted.

"They've been exposed to so much because of their comfort with technology that they are basically idea machines," Rios told CBS News. "AI could be very advantageous for this group, and they have demonstrated their ability to use it for good, so far."

Kayan Shah, a college sophomore and co-founder of Graft Systems, was one of 10 winners of last year's America's Startup competition. He's partnering with vineyards across San Francisco to test and further develop the company's technology, which collects images of plants and combines them with machine-learning models that predict how many grapes they'll yield by analyzing variables such as weather, sunlight and a vineyard's location.
"AI could take over many, many jobs, but this is the status quo, so the only option you have is to make the best of it, and we're using it to help wine growers," Shah said.

While Shah isn't yet 21 and can't legally drink, he said he appreciates wine culture and wants to preserve it, citing a decline in alcohol consumption rates. Americans who say they drink alcohol fell to 54% last year, the lowest level in 90 years, according to an August 2025 Gallup poll.
Skin in the game

Another entrant in last year's startup contest pitched a biotech company that helps people track their exposure to harmful ultraviolet rays and potentially detect skin cancer earlier. Kristina Schiffman, the founder of UV Sense, told CBS News the company uses AI to educate people about their skin, including a tool for analyzing and tracking moles and other conditions.
"We take user inputs, including images and concerns about the skin, and use AI to help people make an informed decision about what they should do," Schiffman said.
"If you have a freckle you're concerned about, you can upload photos and use AI to monitor its shape, size and color, and we can recommend a dermatologist visit," she explained.

Aspiring entrepreneurs can submit their best ideas to America's Startup before applications close on Oct. 8 at 7:59 p.m. EDT. The competition will award a total of $1 million in cash and prizes to a series of winners. Applicant teams can win up to $50,000 each.

An investor council, which will review proposals and have the opportunity to invest, includes some of the nation's most prominent entrepreneurs, such as Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak and Sarah Friar, chief financial officer at ChatGPT developer OpenAI.

title: Congress tried to stop surprise medical bills. It created another problem.
summary: Healthcare providers and middlemen are exploiting a loophole in a 2020 law designed to shield consumers from surprise medical bills.
story: A law designed to protect patients from surprise medical bills succeeded in eliminating unexpected charges, but spawned a lucrative arbitration industry with providers and specialized middlemen extracting payments far above benchmark billing rates.
The practice is ultimately driving up healthcare costs for consumers, a CBS News investigation found.

The arbitration system Congress created to settle disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers allows doctors and resolution specialists acting on their behalf to win payments many times higher than typical rates for medical services. Those costs don't disappear: Much of the money comes from employer-sponsored health plans, meaning workers may ultimately pay through higher premiums or reduced benefits.

Under the arbitration system established by the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, insurers are paying healthcare providers hundreds of dollars for routine lab tests that typically cost between $10 and $30, industry researchers told CBS News. In one instance, a plastic surgeon was awarded more than $400,000 to perform a breast reduction, a procedure the insurer said it had previously paid the doctor between $6,000 and $30,000 to perform.
The plastic surgeon, Dr. Norman Rowe, routinely was awarded around 170 times the benchmark rates for his services under the NSA's arbitration system, a CBS News analysis of public data shows.
A spokesman for Dr. Rowe told CBS News that insurers had manipulated benchmark rates to lowball doctors and create "artificially low reimbursement rates."

"Dr. Rowe uses the widely recognized gold standard FairHealth benchmarks set by the independent nonprofit FairHealth.org using reliable and objective market data. FairHealth data is so reliable that it is incorporated into statutes and regulations around the country and serves as the official data source for many state health programs," the spokesman added.

In addition to the typical benchmark rate arbitrators consider (known as the "qualifying payment amount," or QPA), FairHealth provides another rate that can be used during the dispute resolution process. Medicare rates, meanwhile, may not be considered.

CBS News found that another doctor — Long Island spine surgeon Vadim Lerman — was being awarded an average of 280 times the benchmark rates in arbitration. He declined an interview, but a spokesman for Lerman said that "the suggestion that a physician is receiving 'hundreds of times' above benchmark rates is incorrect. No comparison should be made to the insurer's initial offer — which can be inappropriately low for a complex surgical procedure — and the award given to the physician."
"Baseball-style arbitration"
Insurers have, in many cases, been forced to pay high rates like those Dr. Rowe charges under the law's so-called "baseball-style" or "pendulum" arbitration system.

In an arbitration under the No Surprises Act, insurers and providers each propose a rate for a given service. There's no room for negotiation, as an arbitrator must choose between one of the two parties' suggested figures.

Arbitrators side with providers in more than 85% of the cases, according to Leland Robbins, a product leader at Turquoise Health, a data transparency startup. Some arbitrators – officially called certified Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR, entities – have track records of siding with providers in an even larger share of cases, according to Robbins' group.
He told CBS News that while patients are no longer being surprised by large medical bills, there is a catch to the new system.

"The transaction didn't go away. It went behind closed doors and has moved into this arbitration process when a payer and a provider can't agree what the fair price should be," Robbins said. "Given that 70% of these awards are being taken out of employer-sponsored health plans, consumers are going to start seeing it when it comes time for open enrollment."
He added, "You know, employers are not able to withstand and absorb these kinds of big fees. They're going to be probably not paying for as much of your premiums."

Last year, 15 government-certified arbitrators earned fees per case, with 17 arbitrators designated to do this work today. Each side in the dispute — the healthcare provider and the insurer — pays into the process prior to the arbitrator making any decision.

During the first six months of 2025, insurers and providers submitted 1.2 million new disputes to the arbitration portal, while federal officials had only expected approximately 17,000 cases per year, research from the Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR) at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy shows.
However, HaloMD, a company that files cases on behalf of providers, told CBS News that the initial estimates "were objectively flawed in how they calculated expected volume."
Collectively, arbitrators making the decisions have earned more than $2 billion in fees. None agreed to on-camera interviews with CBS News.
New Jersey House Rep. Frank Pallone, a Democrat and the lead sponsor of the No Surprises Act, blames private equity, in part, for breaking the system he helped create.
He said just a few private equity firms – which are increasingly buying up anesthesiology, radiology and emergency room practices — are driving arbitration cases.

Pallone told CBS News that doctors should be paid the equivalent of in-network rates for the services they provide, but said "we had no choice" but to introduce the arbitration system "if we wanted to actually get rid of surprise billing."
"I knew it was not going to go well, but I didn't know it was going to be this bad," he added.
Dispute resolution cottage industry

The law's arbitration provision has also created an opportunity for intermediaries to guide providers through the process and rake in profits by taking a cut of bills that are up to 1,000% above the benchmark rate for a service, CBS News found. Critics argue that such firms demand more money on providers' behalf, leading to the large settlements that drive up everyone's costs.

HaloMD bills itself as "the expert" in arbitration cases brought under the No Surprises Act. Founded by Texas couple Scott and Alla Laroque in 2022, the same year the No Surprises Act took effect, the company is one of the fledgling industry's biggest players.

Private equity firms also sometimes own both physician staffing firms and Independent Dispute Resolution entities, creating a conflict of interest and undermining the law's fairness. HaloMD is not private equity-backed, but Halo and two other groups with investments from buyout firms collectively handled more than 75% of disputes settled in arbitration last year, according to Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms.

According to Halo, the firm made more than $1 billion for its clients, routinely earning awards that are nine times the benchmark rates for services. Halo takes a cut of the payouts but has not disclosed the amount.

Halo chief external affairs officer Patrick Velliky told CBS News that insurance companies, not firms like his, are responsible for driving up consumer healthcare costs by either not participating in the arbitration process or submitting ludicrously low offers.

"24% of the time, insurers lose by default. They didn't submit an offer at all. Another 9 1/2% of the time, insurers submit an offer, like a dollar or less," Velliky told CBS News. "So what that actually looks like, a patient goes to the E-D with a heart attack, we go to arbitration and the insurer is offering a total of $1.00."

He also said that insurance companies are offering misleading information about the benchmark rate. "Whatever the actual median in-network rate is, it's not what the insurer presented," Velliky told CBS News. "They're miscalculating it."
A federal court sided with providers on the issue this summer, saying the benchmark rate is "artificially low," pulled down by insurers' $0- or $ 1-reimbursement offers to doctors.
Proposed reforms
Pallone wants to reform the law to gut what he sees as the root of the issues arising from the No Surprises Act: arbitration.

He plans to introduce legislation this week to eliminate the arbitration process and stipulate that providers be paid in-network rates, even if they are out-of-network. Pallone's office also told CBS News that so-called ghost rates, which often drag the benchmark rate down, will be excluded from calculations moving forward.

"Whether it's the hospitals, the doctors, the nurse, they're really trying to care for people. Of course, all of them should have a decent income so they can live," the New Jersey lawmaker said. "But why should these outside investors be making all this money off the backs of, you know, your insurance premiums, essentially?"

title: Why you just got a $90 Social Security check — and who missed out
summary: Millions of seniors are getting $90 direct deposits from Social Security this week, prompting questions about the source of the money.
story: Millions of seniors are receiving $90 deposits from the Social Security Administration this week, prompting some to question the source of the money. The checks are tied to the Trump administration's announcement that it would send checks to about 20 million Medicare enrollees to lower healthcare costs.

President Trump on Friday announced that the administration would send the money to some participants in the healthcare plan's Part B, which pays for doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings. About one-third of Medicare Part B's 62.9 million enrollees are eligible, with about 40 million not qualifying for the payments.

The payments are funded by the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress to improve and support the original Medicare fee-for-service program. Experts say the $90, while helpful, won't fully offset higher costs facing Medicare recipients.

Premiums for Part B rose by more than $200 annually in 2026 and are projected to increase by nearly $80 in 2027, according to the Medicare trustees' most recent annual report. The standard monthly premium for Part B in 2026 is $202.90, a figure that's expected to rise to $209.50 next year.
Americans of all ages are grappling with rising healthcare costs, which they cite as a top financial concern, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.
Who qualifies for the $90 checks?

Seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare and who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid are eligible for the one-time payment. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage are ineligible for the payments.
That leaves more than 20 million Part B enrollees who are eligible, according to a CMS fact sheet.

"People who are paying the income-related premium have higher incomes to begin with, so the thinking is that they may be better able to absorb higher costs and wouldn't benefit as much from the $90 payment as people with lower incomes," Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, told CBS News.
Medicare Advantage isn't the same as traditional Medicare, which is likely why those enrollees don't qualify for the payments, she added.
The agency said the initiative improves Medicare and makes coverage more affordable by putting "healthcare dollars back where they belong – in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries."
How will the money be sent?

Most eligible beneficiaries will receive the $90 rebate through a direct deposit from the Social Security Administration on or around Oct. 8, according to the CMS fact sheet. Some seniors reported receiving the payments or pending deposits on Tuesday, according to social media reports.

Some beneficiaries will receive a $90 paper check from the U.S. Department of the Treasury later in October. It will include the following message: "Medicare Improvement Fund Payment; $90 Payment to Offset October Premium."
Some advocates say the paper payments could go unnoticed by seniors, especially given the volume of mail many receive from insurers during open enrollment season.
Why are 40 million people left out?
About 40 million Medicare Part B enrollees are ineligible for the $90 payment. They include:
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plansThose who pay an income-related adjusted premiumPeople who do not live in the U.S.Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans
Those who pay an income-related adjusted premium
People who do not live in the U.S.
Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance

Eligible beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Part B can call 1-800-MEDICARE to determine whether or not they qualify for the one-time check. Beneficiaries who want to check on the status of their payment can call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213 beginning on Oct. 15.
