title: Americans are paying 62% more for water than a decade ago, study finds
summary: Americans paid an average of $531 per year for household water in 2025, although people in some states pay far more, according to a new study.
story: Americans aren't only paying more for food amid stubbornly high inflation — the cost of washing it down has also surged.

Water costs have shot up across the U.S., with a new study by the nonprofit advocacy group Food and Water Watch showing that households are paying 62% more for water at home than a decade ago. Those expenses are rising as utilities invest more in aging infrastructure and in adapting their systems to cope with the effects of climate change, Food and Water Watch said in its study.

Federal support for the nation's water infrastructure has declined. The 2025 Infrastructure Report Card, an evaluation by the American Society of Civil Engineers, said that since fiscal year 2022, Congress has appropriated at least $1 billion below the authorized funding levels for a federal fund that supports state water infrastructure projects.

A 2023 survey by the Environmental Protection Agency projects that drinking water systems across the U.S. will need $625 billion in investment over the next two years to implement upgrades and meet health requirements.

Food and Water Watch based its findings on data from 500 of the largest community water systems around the country that serve a combined 155 million people. More specifically, Food and Water Watch looked at how much utilities charged for 60,000 gallons of water, the estimated amount households use for drinking, showering, laundry and similar purposes in a year. The study did not include bills for wastewater or stormwater, which are managed by separate utilities.
How are water costs changing across the country?

The average water bill across the 500 systems Food and Water Watch studied was $531 last year. However, the amount someone pays can vary widely depending on where they live. The government-run water system in Hempstead, New York, charged people an average of $133 a year last year, the lowest rate of the systems examined in the study.
On the other end of the spectrum is San Jose, California, where the private-sector company San Jose Water charged residents an average of $1,416 in 2025, up 163% from a decade ago, the group found.

The state with the lowest overall bills was Idaho, where three of its largest water systems charged an average of $286 in 2025. West Virginia, which has some of the highest poverty rates in the country, had the highest bills. The two largest systems there, owned by American Water, charged an average of $1,383 a year, according to Food and Water Watch.

Costs were higher in counties where water systems are run by for-profit corporations, the group said. Those private companies charged an average of $823 for water in 2025, $329 more than what the public systems charged.

title: Trump temporarily expands use of red-dyed diesel. Will it lower costs?
summary: Experts say the new executive order will have a limited impact on farmers and truckers who rely on diesel.
story: President Trump's new executive order allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways is aimed at lowering costs for truckers and farmers grappling with diesel prices that remain near record highs. But experts say they are skeptical that the order could deliver sweeping savings.
"It might lead to savings for some, but there are a lot of details that will prevent this from having widespread relief," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News.

Mr. Trump announced the executive order on Tuesday during a midterm rally in Nebraska, saying the move will "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dye diesel for any reason."
Before the EO passed, farmers had to buy regular diesel for their trucks and on-road vehicles, which is subject to excise taxes, a White House official told CBS News in an email.
Now, they can use red-dyed diesel, which is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

The EO comes as diesel prices remain high, although they've eased slightly after reaching a record high last month of $6.53 a gallon. High diesel prices are placing financial strains on the nation's transportation, construction and agricultural industries, which rely heavily on the fuel to move goods and power equipment.
On Tuesday, the national average for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.32, according to AAA, compared to $3.76 before the war in Iran started.
Read on to learn more about red-dyed diesel.
What is red-dyed diesel?
Red-dyed diesel is tax-free diesel intended for off-road vehicles, including farm and construction equipment.

The fuel is dyed red because it allows state law enforcement to easily spot it if drivers are using it on roads and highways in an effort to skirt taxes. Violators may face large fines or penalties, including tax evasion.

Mr. Trump's executive order temporarily removes the limits on red-dyed diesel, allowing all drivers to use it without incurring taxes or penalties. However, it doesn't entirely eliminate taxes on red-dyed diesel.

Instead, it defers the federal excise tax for the remainder of 2026 and directs the Treasury secretary to explore ways to eliminate the requirement to pay the taxes, according to the White House. That means drivers could potentially be on the hook for a payment down the road, experts said.
"Whether anyone who makes the switch to dyed diesel suddenly gets a tax bill is the most unanswered question I have," De Haan said in a post on X.
The White House official said drivers will be liable for the deferred tax only if the Internal Revenue Service, at the direction of the Secretary of the Treasury, takes action to enforce it.
Will the Trump administration's EO lead to cost savings?
According to a White House fact sheet on the executive order, drivers who rely on diesel could save more than $100 each time they fill up.
However, many states also have bans on using red-dyed diesel on roads and highways. The White House said it is working with states to encourage them to also waive the ban.

But if some states don't waive their bans, it could lead to a "convoluted patchwork" of enforcement, which may ultimately deter trucks that need to cross state lines from using red-dyed diesel, De Haan added.

"If one state is enforcing red-dyed diesel and a trucker crosses over with dyed diesel, that could spell trouble, and [lead to] enforcement issues," he said. "Most of the large end users that could stand to benefit from lower prices probably won't get much of the benefit behind this."
The impact on farmers will also be muted, given that they already get tax-free diesel in most states, De Haan noted.
"Most of them have thousands of liters that they've been buying at tax-free, at scheduled intervals, I should say, and so it's not really any huge advantage," he told CBS News.

The EO will allow farmers to use red-dyed diesel in personal vehicles, but it will yield only minimal savings, he added. "I don't think that any farmer is going to be jumping for joy at the prospect of saving, you know, 50 or 60 cents a gallon on their personal vehicle."
Fails to address the supply issue
Experts noted that the EO doesn't address the lack of diesel supply, the key issue keeping prices elevated.
"The U.S. has about 105 million barrels of diesel in  inventory," Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News in an email. "This move doesn't increase or decrease that level."
In theory, the EO should still put downward pressure on diesel prices; however, swings in the diesel market could blunt progress toward lower prices, Kloza added.
Lowering prices without increasing supply could also stimulate demand, which could have the unintended consequence of driving up costs, De Haan pointed out.
"Part of the reason why we have these high prices is because economics is telling us that there are imbalances," he said. "So to ignore them and go ahead with this risks exacerbating the issue."

title: Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: The merger unites two major movie studios, news operations CBS News and CNN and cable networks including Comedy Central and TNT.
story: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting the movie studios behind "The Godfather" and the "Harry Potter" films into a media colossus rebranded as Skydance.
The merger also brings together the news outlets CBS News and CNN, major cable networks such as Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT and the streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.
David Ellison, who orchestrated the merger as CEO of Paramount Skydance, will lead the new company along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who was previously CEO of toy company Mattel.
In an email to employees, Ellison and Kreiz said the merger will allow the company to create a "stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry."
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a separate statement from Skydance.
As part of the deal, Warner Bros. shareholders will receive the cash equivalent of roughly $31 per share, the company said.

The deal came together after Paramount settled a July lawsuit from a coalition of 12 state attorneys general and a separate lawsuit from the Writers Guild of America (WGA). Both had sued to block it on antitrust grounds.

Under the settlement agreement, Paramount pledged to produce 30 films in each of the first two years after the merger and is barred from selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles for at least five years.

Paramount has also agreed to establish an editorial board to "help CNN and CBS maintain editorial independence," according to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office. WGA agreed to settle its lawsuit after Paramount reached a deal with the states.
Ellison and Kreiz said the company is targeting $6 billion in cost savings, a move that some in the media industry are concerned could lead to job losses.
"Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," the co-CEOs said in the email to Skydance employees.

title: Coca-Cola reveals new flavors for Coke, Powerade and other brands
summary: Coca-Cola said it will roll out the new flavors, all fruit-inspired, in 2027. Here's what the beverage giant is planning.
story: Coca-Cola is refreshing its beverage lineup with a series of new fruit flavors.

The company said Monday that it will roll out "innovations" for its Coca-Cola, Fairlife, Mr. Pibb, Powerade and Topo Chico brands starting in 2027. Coca-Cola will showcase the new products at the National Association of Convenience Stores event in Las Vegas, Nevada, this week.

A Coca-Cola spokesperson said the company is also testing several new products in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania to gauge consumer interest in a prebiotic version of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, Sprite Zero Sugar and Fresca.
Coca-Cola fans will have two new flavors to try next year: Coca-Cola Cherry Lime is scheduled to debut in February, and Coca-Cola Strawberry Float will make its premiere in the summer.

The cherry lime product is a new spin on Coca-Cola Cherry, while the strawberry float version appears to be a nod to the popular dessert that blends soda and ice cream. Both come in sugar and zero-sugar options.

Other Coca-Cola beverage brands are also set to get a fruit-inspired refresh next year. Powerade will add watermelon and lemon-lime zero-sugar options in January 2027. Mr. Pibb, a spicy cherry soft drink, will debut "Mr. Pibb Black-Current" in the spring, while a "berry-forward" flavor will be offered for a limited time.

Topo Chico, a carbonated mineral water product, will launch a pineapple-coconut flavor in February, building on its existing lineup of fruit flavors, which include raspberry with lemon, passionfruit and tropical mango, among others.

Core Power protein shakes, sold under the Fairlife brand, will be available in banana and strawberry beginning in January, the first new flavors in almost a decade. Both will contain 26 grams of protein, while the banana flavor will also be available in a 42-gram version.

title: Trump sending ACA and Medicare checks, but will they offset costs?
summary: President Trump sent $500 checks to some Affordable Care Act enrollees, while 20 million Medicare recipients will soon get $90 checks. Will they make a difference?
story: President Trump is sending checks to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees, with the White House describing the efforts as helping to "lower costs" for seniors and families. But experts say the payments may do little to offset rapidly rising healthcare expenses.
On Friday, Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social that his administration this month will send checks of about $90 to more than 20 million Medicare participants in the program's Part B plans.

That announcement followed the White House's Sept. 10 statement that $500 checks would be sent to about 1 million people who enrolled in an ACA plan this year through federal exchanges administered by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The payments, described as refunds for overcharges, are for people who didn't receive ACA insurance subsidies.

"President Trump is delivering on his promises to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans," the White House said in an Oct. 2 statement about the Medicare checks.

While the payments will help defray some of the healthcare costs paid by senior citizens and ACA-enrolled households, the money may not go far enough, health policy experts said. Americans cite healthcare costs as one of their top financial concerns, with almost 30% saying they've skipped or postponed healthcare treatments in the last year because of costs, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.

"A plan to lower healthcare costs is welcome, but President Trump's proposal to provide a one-time $90 payment to some Medicare beneficiaries will likely go unnoticed by most seniors," Max Richtman, CEO of the nonpartisan National Committee to Preserve Social Security & Medicare, told CBS News.
The White House said Mr. Trump is taking action to lower healthcare costs for millions of Americans.

"President Trump is enabling Americans to take control of their health by putting money directly back in the hands of Medicare patients," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said in a statement to CBS News. "In addition to guaranteeing discounted prices on prescription drugs through his Most-Favored-Nation drug pricing agreements, distributing $500 Obamacare Refund checks and increasing price transparency across the board, President Trump is delivering on his promise to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans."

Mr. Trump has also promised $5,000 "dividend" payments to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain electoral control of both the House and Senate after the November midterms. Some economists and other experts have raised doubts about the feasibility of the payments, as they would require Congress to authorize more than $1 trillion in spending and could reignite inflation.
The Trump administration began sending the ACA checks on Sept. 30, while the Medicare checks will be sent starting in early October.
Higher Medicare Part B premiums

Premiums for Medicare Part B, which covers medical services such as doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings, rose by more than $200 annually in 2026, and are forecast to rise by another $79 next year, according to June projections in the Medicare trustees' latest annual report.

That means the $90 check could fall short of covering the increased costs that seniors are already paying this year alone for their Part B plans, according to Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF.

"Receiving a one-time payment of $90 under this new plan from the Trump administration could be helpful, but it may not stretch very far when people are staring down higher costs for gas, heating their homes this coming winter, putting food on the table, keeping up with their mortgage payments," she said.
Rising ACA costs

Meanwhile, the $500 ACA check isn't likely to cover rising costs for people who get their health insurance through the program's marketplaces, said Cynthia Cox, senior vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF.
The average premium for enrollees rose by $780 this year, up 58% from 2025, according to a KFF analysis.

ACA plan costs have risen sharply in 2026, partly due to the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits, which Congress allowed to lapse in December. Those tax breaks had helped lower premium costs for millions of middle-class Americans.

"People this year are paying significantly more than they were paying last year for health insurance on the individual market," Cox told CBS News. "It's going to help some people, certainly — getting a $500 check is better than not getting a $500 check — but for most people it won't cover their full increased costs."

A more effective method to lower healthcare costs would be to restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits, Brian Keyser and Natasha Murphy of the Center for American Progress, a liberal-leaning think tank that supports the ACA, wrote in a Sept. 17 blog post.
Millions left out
About 40 million Medicare Part B recipients don't qualify for the $90 payment, while about 18 million ACA enrollees won't get a $500 check, enrollment data for the programs shows.

The $90 checks will go to seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid. Seniors who are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans are also excluded from the checks, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
The Medicare check is reminiscent of President Trump's proposal to send a $200 drug card to help seniors with out-of-pocket drug costs before the 2020 presidential election, Cubanski said.

While that plan never got off the ground, it was also timed just before an important election. The new Medicare payments, to be disbursed by direct deposit, are set to arrive only weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon and ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, on Saturday called the $90 checks an "attempt to bribe the American public." But experts said the payments may barely register for some seniors.

"There's a question whether many of these payments might go unnoticed," Cubanski added. "People with Medicare get lots of mail from insurance companies and others trying to market plans during the open enrollment season, so this letter might get caught up in all the other mail that people are receiving."

title: When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights for the best deals
summary: Knowing when to buy plane tickets for holiday season travel can save you money. Here's the optimal time to book this year as airfares rise.
story: In trying to score the cheapest airfares for the holidays, when you book a flight often matters just as much as your travel dates. And this year, booking early is particularly important as airfares creep higher, new Google data shows.
Flights for travel around Thanksgiving will be cheapest in October, while people traveling around Christmas should lock in their itineraries by around Halloween, according to Google Flights.
When to book flights for optimal deals

It's best to book as early as possible when your travel dates are relatively fixed. For Thanksgiving, consumers will find the lowest fares 34 days before departure, according to Google Flights, which based its findings on five years of flight data. Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, making Oct. 22 the best day to book travel for the Wednesday before the holiday. For the lowest fares on Turkey Day trips, travelers should aim to purchase tickets between 57 and 21 days before departure.

For flights around Christmas, the lowest fares will be available 56 days before departure. Travelers can land better deals between 33 and 67 days before their trips, according to Google Flights (as of Oct. 5, there are roughly 80 days before Christmas). The best flight deals will emerge between late October and mid-November, according to Google.
Other ways to save

To save money on flights, experts also recommend traveling off-peak, when fewer people will swarm the nation's airports. Data from the fare aggregator Hopper shows that traveling on Monday or Tuesday before Thanksgiving, rather than on Wednesday, can yield savings. Avoid returning on Sunday, Nov. 29, the company said.
The same advice applies around Christmas. Hopper advises avoiding flying on Dec. 18, 19 and 20 and on Dec. 27, the Sunday after Christmas Day.

Americans should expect higher-than-usual flight prices due to the Iran war, which has raised oil and jet fuel prices, the largest expense for airlines after personnel. Before the Middle East conflict began in late February, jet fuel averaged $99 per barrel globally, according to the International Air Transport Association. It peaked at $209 in April and hit $195 a barrel in mid-September, IATA said, citing data from S&P Global Energy Platts.
Hopper data shows that domestic round-trip airfares for Thanksgiving are averaging $402, up 31% from last year. Domestic round-trip Christmas flights are averaging $452, up 23%  from last year.

title: Gatorade sold in dozens of states recalled due to undeclared dyes
summary: Recalled Gatorade sold in 37 states could cause temporary "adverse health consequences," a federal regulatory agency says.
story: PepsiCo has recalled roughly 122,000 cases of Gatorade sold across the U.S. because the product contains undeclared dyes, the Food and Drug Administration said in a notice.

The recall affects cases with 28-ounce bottles of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Gatorade Lemon Lime Zero, Gatorade Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero that were sold in 37 states. The FDA said the beverages contain undeclared Yellow No. 6 and/or Yellow No. 5, artificial dyes that affect the product's color.

PepsiCo initiated the recall on Sept. 25. On Oct. 2, the FDA updated the recall to Class II, which means that exposure to the product "may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences," according to the regulatory agency.

The cases of Gatorade were sold in Alaska, Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin.
The recall number is H-0009-2027.
PepsiCo did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether customers who bought the recalled Gatorade are eligible for a refund.

title: Environmental groups sue Trump administration over vehicle MPG rollback
summary: Reducing fuel-efficiency standards will raise prices at the pump and produce more harmful emissions, according to environmentalists.
story: Environmental groups filed a lawsuit on Friday against the Trump administration over its rollback of vehicle fuel efficiency standards, saying the move will increase gasoline consumption and boost prices at the pump for U.S. motorists.

"It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air," Katherine Garcia, Sierra Club's Clean Transportation for All Director, said in a statement.

The new Trump administration rules, announced on Monday, changed the Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards, which dictate how many miles per gallon vehicles must be able to travel. Under the revised standards, automakers must achieve a fleetwide average of 34.9 miles per gallon by 2031, down from a projected 50.4 miles under rules previously implemented by the Biden administration.

In announcing the new CAFE standards, the Department of Transportation said it will lower the average upfront cost of new vehicles by $1,300, cut annual oil consumption and give automakers more choice regarding the types of cars they manufacture. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also said the revamped rule will blunt the "illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn't want."
But the groups behind the lawsuit allege that reducing fuel efficiency will raise costs for drivers and increase vehicle emissions, a leading cause of climate change.

"Consumers need more fuel-efficient choices when considering new cars, and they deserve vehicles that get more miles per gallon and miles per dollar," Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group and a plaintiff in the suit, said in a statement.
Other groups joining the legal action include the Center for Biological Diversity's Climate Law Institute, Conservation Law Foundation and Environmental Defense Fund.

A typical passenger vehicle emits 4.6 metric tons of carbon dioxide, a major greenhouse gas, per year, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. As of 2022, the most recent year for which data is available, the transportation industry accounted for 28% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, the agency says.
The national average price for a gallon of gasoline on Friday was $4.40, up from $3.16 a year ago and from roughly $2.98 just before the Iran war started in late February.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review on Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the CAFE rules.
The Transportation Department and NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment by The Associated Press.
Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the energy crisis of the 1970s, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

title: American Airlines will let travelers mix cash and miles to pay for flights
summary: As holiday airfares spike, American Airlines plans to let travelers pay for flights with a mix of cash and loyalty points.
story: American Airlines customers will soon be able to mix cash and airline miles to pay for flights.

The carrier announced the new policy in a memo to customers on Friday, explaining that it will soon offer travelers more flexibility in covering trip costs. U.S. members of American's AAdvantage loyalty program will be able to combine cash and miles to pay for domestic trips.
Flights to and from Alaska and Hawaii are excluded from the offer, while American said it plans to expand the offering to more routes.

American said it will roll out the feature in the coming weeks, without specifying when it plans to implement the policy. American billed the change as a way for customers to get more value from their memberships.

AAdvantage members will be able to book flights using cash and miles on American's website or mobile app. Once logged in to their loyalty account, members will be instructed to choose their desired flights first. On the checkout screen, members' available cash and miles options will be shown.

Customers will use an interactive slider to choose the combination of cash and miles to apply toward their purchase. American rivals Delta Air Lines and United Airlines already offer similar flexible payment options.

American Airlines also announced this week a limited-time promotion aimed at expanding its market share, under which travelers with status on competing airlines are granted the equivalent status tier on American flights. To qualify, travelers must submit proof of their status with Delta SkyMiles, JetBlue TrueBlue or other reward programs. American will then issue an "Instant Status Pass," valid for four months.
Airline ticket prices have jumped following the war in Iran, which has reduced global oil supplies and driven up jet fuel costs. Jet fuel accounts for up to 30% of carriers' operating costs.

Airfares this holiday season are expected to reach a 10-year high, according to Hopper. The fare aggregator found that round-trip flight prices around Thanksgiving are already up 31% compared to last year.

title: Amazon vows to invest $1 billion in areas where it builds data centers
summary: Amazon said it will invest $1 billion over five years to support job education, energy affordability and other priorities in communities where its data centers are located.
story: Amazon's cloud computing division on Friday announced a new effort to temper opposition to data centers in some U.S. communities, while saying the U.S. "can't afford to lose" the race to dominate artificial intelligence globally.

The tech giant pledged to invest an additional $1 billion over five years in the communities where it builds data centers, the facilities that power AI, on top of existing commitments. Amazon said the money will go toward education, job training, energy affordability, and water and energy preservation, and also fund other local priorities.

"There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren't the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run," Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said in a blog post. "The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation's focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so."
A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor data centers in their areas, largely because they perceive the facilities as harming the environment and draining local resources.

A report from Schneider Electric, a company specializing in digital automation and energy management, projects that U.S. electricity demand will increase by 16% by 2029, mainly due to the proliferation of data centers. AI searches use 10 times more electricity than normal internet searches, according to a study from the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit organization.

According to a group called Data Center Watch, which tracks opposition to data centers across the U.S., 30  states have introduced or adopted legislation or taken other actions to address some of these concerns. Some communities also imposed preemptive moratoriums on data center construction even before builders planned sites, the group notes.

The number of data centers in the U.S. nearly doubled between 2021 and 2024, according to a report from Environment America, a network of environmental groups. Grassroots efforts to block data center development have thwarted at least 45 developments across 27 states, valued at $68 billion, according to the group.

Amazon's Garman said such disruption is dangerous, claiming that the data center buildout is so geopolitically important that foreign nations could be "intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down."

title: Employers added 29,000 jobs in September, missing economic forecasts
summary: Unemployment ticked up to 4.2% in September, while employers pulled back on hiring amid economic headwinds.
story: Employers across the U.S. added 29,000 jobs in September, below economists' forecasts and signaling that some businesses are holding off on hiring amid headwinds such as surging energy prices and higher inflation.

Economists had forecast the economy would add 90,000 new jobs last month, according to financial data firm FactSet. The unemployment rate stood at 4.2% in September, up slightly from 4.1% in the prior month.
Cooler hiring in July and August

Recent data suggest the labor market has picked up since last year, when employers added an average of just 10,000 new jobs per month. But the September report suggests that hiring may be flagging after August's strong employment report and the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hike in three years.

"September's nonfarm payroll gain of just 29,000 jobs raises questions about the durability of the labor market after the Federal Reserve's first interest rate increase since 2023," Jerry Tempelman, vice president of economic and fixed income research at Mutual of America, said in an email.

Hiring was muted across industries, with even healthcare, this year's bright spot in job growth, adding just 17,000 new hires, experts noted. Financial services firms, meanwhile, shed 7,000 jobs last month.

"Only healthcare and construction were hiring, and it was weak," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now. "Across America, people don't like this labor market. It's not hard to see why. There's still not much hiring going on."

The Labor Department on Friday also revised down the payroll gains for July and August by a combined 60,000. The downward revisions put August's "rebound into perspective," said Steve Rick, chief economist at financial services firm TruStage, in an email. "One month doesn't make a trend, and monthly payroll numbers can bounce around quite a bit. What matters more is whether the three-month trend continues to show a labor market that is gradually cooling rather than falling off a cliff."

Economists are closely watching other measures of labor market strength, such as wage growth, which has lagged inflation for five consecutive months. In September, wages rose at an annual rate of 3%, below the August Consumer Price Index reading of 3.4%. The September CPI data will be released on Oct. 14.
September's wage growth is "the lowest since May 2021," Long said. "Inflation has wiped out wage gains since March. That's a real financial squeeze."

Data released Thursday by outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas shows that job cuts have fallen sharply in 2026. Layoffs through September have declined 40% from the same period a year earlier, its report found. On a monthly basis, layoffs dropped 20% compared with September 2025, marking the lowest level in four years.
What it means for interest rates

The increase in the nation's unemployment rate "warrants close attention," Tempelman said. Rising joblessness combined with softer hiring could signal that additional Fed interest rate hikes could constrain economic activity, he added.

The weaker-than-expected September jobs data could cause the Federal Reserve to hold off on an additional rate cut at its October meeting, said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, in an email.

"For the Fed, these numbers do not make a case for a rate increase in October," he said. "A hike would have to come from the inflation data, not from a labor market that produced 29,000 jobs against a 90,000 estimate and then subtracted 60,000 from the prior two months."

A stable labor market gives the Federal Reserve more room to raise interest rates in the coming months, according to economists. The central bank is focused on driving inflation down to its 2% annual target and last month raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in more than three years.
In August, U.S. inflation rose at an annual rate of 3.4%, as soaring energy costs pushed up consumer prices.

title: Amazon Prime customers could get $200 refunds in expanded FTC deal
summary: Some Amazon customers could receive refunds of up to $200. Here's who is eligible for a payment and when consumers will get the money.
story: Amazon is issuing refunds to eligible Amazon customers under a revised $2.5 billion settlement with the Federal Trade Commission to resolve allegations that the retailer deceptively enrolled customers in its Prime subscription service.

The FTC said last month that more consumers qualify for refunds from Amazon and also raised the maximum payment from $51 to $200. As of September, Amazon had refunded more than $845 million to customers, with the company agreeing under the settlement to issue $1.5 billion in refunds and pay a $1 billion civil penalty.
Who is newly eligible for a refund?

The FTC's original order in September 2025 required only that Amazon refund customers who used fewer than 10 Prime benefits, such as free shipping, over the course of one year. The revised order requires Amazon to reimburse members who used up to 20 Prime benefits over a year and who signed up for Prime between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025.
When will Amazon customers get their money?

Amazon began issuing automatic payments to additional customers on Thursday. Millions of customers used up to 20 Prime benefits, and are newly eligible for payouts of up to $200, according to the FTC.

If payments don't meet a required threshold by February 2027, Amazon will automatically disburse an additional $149 to consumers who previously received refunds under the settlement. All eligible customers will receive refunds by April 2027.
How will refunds be made?
Amazon is making the payments electronically, either through Venmo or PayPal, or by mailing checks to consumers.
Consumers are not required to submit refund claims, respond to any notices or complete any paperwork, according to the FTC.

Amazon is responsible for administering the refunds, the FTC noted, saying that the agency is not contacting customers about the matter. Anyone posing as the FTC trying to reach consumers about the Amazon settlement is likely a scammer, the commission said.

title: Democrats invest more heavily in Gina Hinojosa as Pritzker offers support
summary: Last week, more than 70 Latino Democratic leaders sent a letter to Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the DGA, urging the group to invest $10 million to help Hinojosa's campaign.
story: National Democrats are stepping up their financial support for Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa after recent polls showed a dead heat and more Democrats began to see an opportunity to potentially defeat three-term incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, a possible 2028 presidential contender, and the Democratic Governors Association are each putting at least $1 million behind Hinojosa, according to sources familiar with the investments and a senior DGA official. Pritzker's contribution is actually larger — $1.2 million, according to sources familiar with the commitment. The New York Times first reported the investment.

The infusion comes at a crucial point for Hinojosa's campaign. She reported roughly $4 million in cash on hand at the end of last month, according to campaign finance filings, and her campaign said it had been outspent by Abbott by roughly 10-to-1.
In a statement, Hinojosa's campaign said her campaign has "momentum," and said "we're grateful for the support we've received in this final stretch from leaders across the country."

Last week, more than 70 Latino Democratic leaders sent a letter to Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the DGA, urging the group to invest $10 million to help Hinojosa's campaign. A source told CBS News on Wednesday that the state's Latino leaders, including Texas congressional lawmakers, met with the DGA to increase pressure to fund Hinojosa's campaign, which was first reported by NBC News.
A source familiar with the investments tells CBS News that the DGA took action to support Hinojosa after Pritzker committed his own money to the race.

A DGA official disputed that characterization, saying that Beshear told Hinojosa in a conversation on Tuesday of last week that the DGA would spend at least $1 million on her campaign. A source close to Hinojosa's campaign confirmed the conversation between Beshear and Hinojosa took place, as well as the Kentucky governor's $1 million  commitment.
Abbott's campaign said in a statement that she is "taking her campaign to out-of-state Democrat strongholds."

Abbott has significantly outraised Hinojosa, including from July to September, when his campaign said it brought in $20 million to her campaign's $13 million. But his campaign reported having $17 million cash on hand, indicating a huge amount of spending given the over $100 million on hand he reported at the beginning of the year.

A Democrat has not been elected to the governor's mansion in Texas since Ann Richards in 1990, who lost reelection to George W. Bush four years later, and President Trump won the state by more than 13 points in 2024. Abbott had not been considered vulnerable, but recent polls had shown the race tightening.
Mr. Trump is campaigning in San Antonio on Wednesday with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and several other GOP candidates, although Abbott is not joining the rally.

title: Obama hosts fundraiser with Senate Democrats weeks before midterms
summary: Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.
story: Washington – Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.
The event featured a conversation between Obama and Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, vice chair of the DSCC, about Democrats' efforts to flip the Senate.

"I think he is just such a voice for our country, and of both realism and practical optimism, and I think we need that right now," Blunt Rochester told CBS News. "And I think he also lays the foundation for the significance of this election."

Senate Democrats have become increasingly optimistic about their prospects this fall after several races shifted toward the party in recent weeks, including in deep-red states like Texas and Ohio that are considered toss-ups, according to CBS News' battleground tracker.

"We do not want to be overconfident, but what we're seeing in state after state after state is that people are sick of Trump, they're sick of the Republican Senate going along with them, and they see the clear divisions we have drawn between what we stand for and what they stand for," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told CBS News last month. "That has put us on the edge of victory."
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Democrats would need to pick up four seats to gain control of the upper chamber.
Meanwhile, Republicans have argued they still have a path to hold on to the Senate.

"Right now, there's a lot of noise, there always is in the political atmosphere — some of it's created by our opponents," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, told reporters before the body went on recess. "But if we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."

One key target for both parties is Michigan. Democrats are trying to hold the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters while Republicans see it as a prime pickup opportunity. An exclusive CBS Detroit poll, conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications, shows Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with a narrow advantage over GOP challenger and former Rep. Mike Rogers.

Obama is expected to campaign with El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates in the Wolverine State later this month. A source familiar with the former president's thinking said his strategy this fall is "driven by where he can move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters."

The former president has also taped two dozen ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates around the country. Last month, he participated in the second of two fundraisers with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, where he pressed Democrats to do more on the issue of artificial intelligence.

"Certainly if I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, 'Here's our plan for safety, here's our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,'" Obama said. "I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding: What does it mean if there's going to be job displacement? Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?"

Jeffries told CBS News he has remained in contact with Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris and expects both to be engaged through Election Day. The minority leader, who is poised to become the first Black House speaker if Democrats win control of the lower chamber, predicted that House Democrats would "take back the majority" this fall.
"It's an all-hands-on-deck effort," Jeffries said.

title: Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait
summary: CBS News obtained new video from a person on the ground showing an Iranian attack on a U.S. base at the beginning of the war.
story: Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.

The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.

The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.
The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.

"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.
Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.
CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.

Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.

Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.
"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."

While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.

"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."

A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.

The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.

No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.
"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"

The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.

In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

title: Protesters ejected from raucous Trump rally in Texas
summary: Several hecklers were removed from President Trump's rally in Texas late Wednesday, drawing jeers from the crowd as the president made fun of the protesters.
story: Several hecklers were removed from President Trump's rally in Texas late Wednesday.

At least 10 people were either ejected from the venue by authorities or appeared to walk out after interrupting the rally, drawing jeers from the crowd at San Antonio's Freeman Coliseum as Mr. Trump mocked the protesters. It's the president's third trip to Texas in recent weeks to support Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who is facing a tougher-than-expected contest against Democratic candidate James Talarico.

Less than 10 minutes into Mr. Trump's speech, a person stormed away from the stage while yelling. At one point, a man in a red hat grabbed that person's hair and appeared to get into a physical altercation, leading other rallygoers to separate the two. After the person walked out of the venue, the president asked: "Is there anything like a Trump rally?"
"He's going back home to mom right now," the president said. "What he doesn't know is that his mom voted for Trump."

For the next hour, several other people were walked out of the venue by law enforcement or security while the crowd booed them. In some cases, Trump supporters and demonstrators were separated after physically tangling with each other.
At least one person was handcuffed before law enforcement led him out.
The president poked fun at several of the attendees who were ejected, saying one person has "got to lose a lot of weight" and others were "really bad-looking people."
CBS News has reached out to local authorities and the U.S. Secret Service for more information on the ejections.

Mr. Trump was on stage for well over an hour. He spent much of the event railing against Talarico, a state lawmaker who is aiming to be the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. Most polls show Talarico either with a narrow edge or neck-and-neck with Paxton, a state attorney general with a polarizing record who frustrated other Republicans by ousting Sen. John Cornyn in a primary earlier this year.

Republicans have sought to cast Talarico as too liberal for Texas, a theme that Mr. Trump emphasized throughout the evening, jabbing Talarico for his record in the state legislature. The president said if Talarico wins, he would turn Texas into a "dirty, failing, crime-ridden third-world dumping ground."

Mr. Trump also spent a large amount of time on immigration, touting the precipitous drop in unauthorized border crossings in recent years. The issue dominated Mr. Trump's 2024 campaign but has become more challenging for him as most voters grow skeptical of his administration's hardline enforcement tactics — particularly Hispanic voters, whose shift toward Mr. Trump helped propel him to victory in 2024.

title: Mamdani criticized for statement mourning Oct. 7 and condemning Israel
summary: A statement by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani that recognized three years since Hamas' "horrific" attack on Israel — and criticized Israel's "ongoing genocide" in Gaza — has drawn fury from some Democrats.
story: A statement by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani that recognized three years since Hamas' "horrific" attack on Israel — and extensively criticized Israel's "ongoing genocide" in the Gaza Strip — has drawn fury from some Democrats.

Mamdani is a longstanding and vehement critic of Israel's actions during its war with Hamas in Gaza, and an opponent of U.S. aid to Israel — issues that have divided Democrats nationwide and drawn criticism for the mayor from moderates, leaders of Jewish groups and Israeli officials. Mamdani has long defended his stance, saying criticism of Israel is distinct from antisemitism.

Wednesday's statement by Mamdani began by calling it a "profoundly painful" day for many New Yorkers, noting Hamas' "horrific war crimes" on Oct. 7, 2023, including the killing of about 1,200 people in Israel and the taking of more than 250 hostages. He added: "We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."

The mayor then shifted to criticizing Israel for its "devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza" — noting the more than 74,000 deaths recorded in the enclave, according to the Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry.
"Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes," Mamdani said.

"Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment," Mamdani added.
Several Democratic elected officials blasted Mamdani's statement, arguing it was too focused on Israel rather than Hamas.

Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida accused Mamdani of "desecrating the memory of murdered, innocent Jews," Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey said the mayor was "blam[ing] the victims" of the Oct. 7 attack, and Jersey City Mayor Steven Fulop called the statement "inappropriate and unnecessarily inflammatory."

Rep. Richie Torres, a Democrat who represents the Bronx, penned an X post that did not name Mamdani, but said: "Perhaps, for just one day—October 7th—the critics of Israel could take a vacation from their hysterical hatred of the world's only Jewish State and find it within themselves to express condolences for the thousands of Israelis murdered, maimed, mutilated, raped, and abducted at the hands of Hamas."
Rep. Daniel Goldman — who lost a Democratic primary in his Manhattan and Brooklyn district to Mamdani-endorsed Brad Lander earlier this year — called the mayor's message "reprehensible."

"In the guise of 'grieving' with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with," Goldman wrote on X.
Lander, the Democratic nominee in Goldman's deep-blue district, wrote a statement of his own on Tuesday that condemned Hamas but argued against the "flattening of empathy."
"We can mourn for those lost on October 7th and still acknowledge the enormous imbalance of power between Israel and the Palestinians," Lander wrote in a post on Substack.

Mamdani also faced pushback from the Anti-Defamation League, whose CEO, Jonathan Greenblatt, is a frequent critic of the mayor. Greenblatt wrote on social media that in Mamdani's statement, "not once do you say 'Jews.'"
"You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points," Greenblatt wrote.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called Mamdani's statement an "outrageous & disgusting rant," while Ofir Akunis, Israeli consul general in New York, called it a "disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered."
CBS News has reached out to Mamdani's office.
Mamdani's stance on Israel has drawn intense scrutiny — and applause from his allies — since he began his unexpected ascent to the mayor's office.

Ahead of the 2025 Democratic mayoral primary, Mamdani vowed that if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited New York City, he would seek Netanyahu's arrest on an International Criminal Court warrant accusing him of war crimes.

Over the summer, Mamdani conceded that the city did not have the power to execute the warrant. The U.S. is not a party to the global treaty that created the ICC and generally does not recognize its authority. Israel has called the war crimes allegations "absurd and false."
When Netanyahu visited the city last month to address the United Nations General Assembly, he accused Mamdani of antisemitism and said "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
"Shame on you for distorting the facts, shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor, shame on you for spitting in the face of truth," Netanyahu said.
Mamdani has long rejected allegations that his strong criticisms of Israel have fueled antisemitism, and says the city "has no room for hate or bigotry of any kind."
Last month, Mamdani unveiled a plan to combat antisemitism, including a dedicated antisemitism hotline and funding to upgrade security at synagogues.

Asked by CBS News New York about the criticism he has faced and whether he believes he should dial back his statements, Mamdani said last month: "I think criticism of a prime minister, criticism of government policy is distinct from bigotry of a people. … And what my job is to ensure is not only that we are proud of being the most Jewish city in the United States of America, but that we also make this a city where Jewish life can continue to flourish."

title: Maduro expected to face new charges of torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons
summary: An attorney for Maduro told CBS News that he has not been given notice that additional charges could be coming.
story: Federal prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, for allegedly torturing Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to multiple sources familiar with the case.

The sources said that additional people could be charged in their role for the torture of more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government while Maduro was in power.
One source said the new charges could be announced as soon as Thursday.
Barry Pollack, an attorney for Maduro, told CBS News that he has not been provided any notice that additional charges could be coming.
Flores is due in federal court on Thursday in the Southern District of New York for a bond hearing, and a trial date has been tentatively set for June 2027.
CNN was first to report the potential new charges.
A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government. The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty.
Prosecutors said Maduro was at the "forefront of the corruption" and that he and his associates worked with drug traffickers and narco-terrorists to flood the U.S. with drugs.

Maduro faces four charges: narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
The case against them was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.

Maduro and his wife have asked U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leaders of a foreign country. The judge has not heard arguments on those motions yet.

In September, Alex Saab, a former minister of industry in Maduro's government, pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering tied to an alleged bribery conspiracy and agreed to cooperate in ongoing federal investigations into the regime after being deported to the U.S. from Venezuela.
In May, CBS News reported that federal prosecutors in Miami were ordered to open a new criminal investigation into Maduro amid some concerns that the pending prosecution against him is weak.

title: Trump pitches Trump International Golf Course for site of "presidential retreat"
summary: It's not yet clear what the taxpayer benefit would be for such a build, or how much it would cost.
story: Washington — President Trump on Wednesday claimed the U.S. Secret Service and U.S. military suggested developing Trump International Golf Course in West Palm Beach as a presidential getaway. It would be "like sort of a Camp David retreat" for future presidents, Mr. Trump said.

"This was suggested to me by the military and Secret Service," the president said during an unrelated event in the Oval Office. "There are no high buildings looming over it. There are no houses on it so you don't have houses — we have to inspect rooms. Seems that all presidents play golf."

A White House official said Wednesday that the "United States government has asked to look into developing a presidential retreat" at the golf course so future presidents can "hold important meetings and utilize the amenities of a world-class property."

Trump International Golf Course is where Mr. Trump plays golf when he's staying at his resort at Mar-a-Lago. The Palm Beach Post first reported that an attorney for the golf course wrote a letter to Palm Beach County commissioners offering to designate the golf club as a presidential retreat that could also be used by foreign heads of state.

"The United States government has asked to look into developing a presidential retreat at Trump International Golf Course in Palm Beach for future presidents, so they can hold important meetings and utilize the amenities of a world-class property," the White House official said. "The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly-rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat."
The White House official's statement did not specify whose idea the retreat was first, or whose permission they're seeking.
The cost of the proposed development — and who would bear it — has not been disclosed.
In December, the president is hosting the G20 summit of world leaders at a different property, Trump National Doral Miami.
The Secret Service has paid the Trump Organization hundreds of thousands of dollars to stay at the president's properties during his presidency.

Emma  Nicholson
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Union alleges Bureau of Prisons in contempt for failing to reinstate collective bargaining agreement
summary: Last week, a judge in Connecticut blocked the Bureau of Prisons from terminating its collective bargaining agreement.
story: The union representing 30,000 Bureau of Prisons employees is asking a federal judge to hold the agency in contempt, alleging that prison leadership has refused to follow the court's order to immediately restore its collective bargaining agreement.

The contempt request, filed Oct. 6, comes just one week after U.S. District Judge Vernon Oliver in Connecticut granted a motion for a preliminary injunction against the Bureau of Prisons that was sought by the National Council of Prison Locals.

Bureau of Prisons Director William Marshall terminated the collective bargaining agreement on Sept. 25, 2025. He alleged the union posed an "obstacle to progress" and said it was not the "kind of union" he could support.

The judge ruled that the union was likely to succeed on the merits of its argument that the BOP had violated the Administrative Procedure Act by terminating the collective bargaining agreement and ordered the bureau to reinstate it immediately.

In its motion for contempt, the union alleged that bureau leadership is stonewalling and refusing to allow the union to resume its usual operations, including by allowing people to have "official" union time.
In one such example, the motion and an accompanying sworn statement said that a BOP employee who was facing termination asked to be represented by a shop steward at the meeting.
"There ain't no union," a BOP official allegedly told the employee, according to the motion. The employee was terminated on Oct. 5.

In another allegation, the union said that Marshall told people on Sept. 29, hours before the court ruling hit the docket, that he had no plans to enforce the terms of the collective bargaining agreement unless he received direct orders from the White House.

"They have not restored union office space or official time, allowed for union representation in disciplinary proceedings, or taken any of the other myriad specific steps that Defendants themselves told the court would be required if the court entered the requested injunction," attorneys for the union wrote.
"Defendants' noncompliance is total."

In a press release issued by American Federation of Government Employees Local 1237, which represents employees at FCI Mendota, the union alleged that management in that facility had also locked union officials out of their offices.
The Bureau of Prisons declined to comment, citing the pending litigation.
Since the court's original Sept. 29 order granting the union's request for a preliminary injunction, the Justice Department has not formally sought a stay to pause the ruling.
On Oct. 2, however, the Justice Department filed a formal "notice of compliance" with the court. In that filing, it said BOP was "aware" of the court's order and "complying with its terms."

But at the same time, the department also said that it did not understand the court's ruling to mean that the BOP could not proceed with trying to re-terminate the collective bargaining agreement again before it expires in May 2028.
It also added that the Justice Department did not expect the U.S. District Court would be supervising "every alleged failure" by BOP to comply with the collective bargaining agreement.
The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate unions at multiple federal agencies.

In March 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that sought to exclude federal offices involved in national security or intelligence work from having collective bargaining agreements with staff. That order also applied to the Justice Department, which includes the Bureau of Prisons.
But after the order was made public, the BOP allowed its union to continue operating for approximately six months before terminating the collective bargaining agreement.
In doing so, Marshall at the time did not cite national security as a basis for his decision.
