title: Isaias becomes first hurricane of 2026 Atlantic season, threatens Gulf Coast
summary: Hurricane Isaias developed late Wednesday as the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026, taking aim at the Gulf Coast from Mississippi to the Florida Panhandle.
story: Hurricane Isaias strengthened from a tropical storm late Wednesday night and is expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast this weekend, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season.
A hurricane warning was issued Wednesday for the northern Gulf Coast, from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, across Alabama to Florida's Bay/Gulf County line.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in his state, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties.
Maps show hurricane's path
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 75 mph and was located about 460 miles southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Forecasters said they expected Hurricane Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday,
"Isaias is expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday," the National Hurricane Center said. "A life-threatening storm surge is expected."

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to Ocean Springs, and from the Bay/Gulf County line to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida.

The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places along the coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall.
The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.
The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late-June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early- to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

Nikki  Nolan

title: Man eyed Mall of America for attack, pledged allegiance to ISIS, FBI says
summary: An 18-year-old Twin Cities man accused of telling an FBI informant he planned to carry out an attack later this month at Mall of America was arrested at gunpoint Tuesday in Richfield, Minnesota, during an arranged meeting to buy an assault rifle, according to a federal criminal complaint filed Wednesday.
story: An 18-year-old man accused of telling an FBI informant he planned to carry out an attack later this month at Mall of America was arrested at gunpoint Tuesday in Richfield, Minnesota, during an arranged meeting to buy an assault rifle, according to a federal criminal complaint filed Wednesday.

Minnesota U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen and FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher Dotson discussed the case involving Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, a Twin Cities resident and U.S. citizen, in a news conference Wednesday afternoon, where Rosen praised the FBI for its "diligence" in thwarting the attack.
"They were able to detect a threat and disrupt it before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people," Rosen said.

In the complaint, authorities say a "confidential human source" exchanged "hundreds of bi-directional messages through multiple social media and encrypted messaging applications" with Mohamud from December 2024 until Tuesday. In those exchanges, Mohamud allegedly "expressed his desire to travel to Somalia" to join al-Shabaab and "fight on its behalf and/or commit a mass casualty attack" in Minnesota.

"The messages this defendant allegedly sent to others were chilling. They document the idolization of ideologically motivated violence, a callous disregard to the sanctity of human life, a blind hatred of people of other faiths and a cold commitment to carrying out his vision of violence in our community," Dotson said. "Mohamud allegedly sought martyrdom in carrying out his plans to murder innocent civilians."
The complaint says the FBI contacted Mohamud's parents in May 2025, but they weren't cooperative.

"The FBI attempted to speak with his parents having seen that this young man was becoming radicalized, and those attempts were rebuffed by the parents," Rosen said. "I just would say to parents all over Minnesota and, for that matter all over America, if you get the indication, especially if you hear from federal law enforcement, that your son or daughter is being radicalized to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, heed those warnings."

In July, Mohamud told an informant he didn't have enough money to go to Somalia, according to the complaint. He allegedly said he would attack in the United States instead, and that if he did, he wasn't doing it "for any worldly matter" but "for the sake of Allah only."

Mohamud allegedly went on to say in a direct message to the source that he considered carrying out an attack at Mall of America in Bloomington or Valleyfair amusement park in Shakopee. An FBI affidavit says he wrote that he might buy two pistols online first.

The complaint says Mohamud said he wanted to attack the mall "because it's owned by Jewish." He said he was inspired in part by last year's deadly antisemitic attack at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia.
Last month, Mohamud told the source he wanted to carry out an attack at the mall during the Hmong Arts Celebration on Oct. 24, saying "it will be a lot of people," according to court documents.
In another message last month, the affidavit says Mohamud wrote that he had been watching video of the 2016 attack at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando, Florida, and thought he could do the same.
"I just walk in and shoot," Mohamud   wrote, according to the complaint.
Court documents also note Mohamud sent the source a video on Discord in which he allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS.

On Tuesday, Mohamud was arrested during an arranged meeting with the source in the parking lot of a Richfield park, according to Rosen. The affidavit says he had left an undercover employee's vehicle with the rifle, four magazines and 200 rounds of ammunition when he was arrested. The filing describes the weapon as a Norinco AK-47 assault rifle, model Mac-90 Sporter, and the ammunition as about 200 live rounds of 7.62x39-caliber.
A Richfield man says he witnessed the arrest during a visit to the dog park.
"They flew out of their vehicle and one of the FBI agents kicked my door shut," said Mike O'Brien. "I was just trying to go to the dog park"
O'Brien says he saw a swarm of up to 30 agents take down a suspect.

"They became aware that this was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched, and in fact, in this young man's case, that radicalization progressed to the point where he planned in the most serious of ways to carry out a mass casualty attack," Rosen said.

Authorities allege Mohamud "knowingly received a firearm and ammunition" with reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and a federal crime of terrorism, including providing or conspiring to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.
Mohamud made his first court appearance Wednesday.

Simon Osamoh previously served as the head of counterterrorism for the Mall of America, now he is the CEO of Kingswood Security Consulting. Osamoh says with tens of millions of visitors each year, and its proximity to transit and the airport, the mall has been a known target in the past.
"Terrorists, or people with that sort of ideology, they favor places of mass gathering which Mall of America is," he said.
Osamoh said the mall has close connections with law enforcement and layers of security pointing to facial recognition, K9 teams and undercover officers.
"I was incredibly concerned but I wasn't surprised," Osmoh said of the alleged plot.
He referred to Minnesota cases just over a decade old, involving men inspired to join foreign terror groups.

Prosecutors accused a group of Somali Americans of plotting to join ISIS overseas. Some were caught trying to fly to Syria. Three men were later convicted at trial in Minnesota, others pleaded guilty.
"I think what Mall of America will be doing in 24, 48 hours is say did we miss anything?" said Osamoh. "Was there anything that we missed that could have identified this individual earlier?"

"We are grateful to the FBI and its law enforcement partners for their vigilance and extraordinary investigative work in identifying, disrupting and removing this threat and protecting the community we all share," the mall said in a statement. "The safety and security of everyone who visits and works at Mall of America has always been our highest priority."

title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend
summary: Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf and is expected to become a hurricane by Thursday before approaching the U.S. northern Gulf Coast on Friday, according to forecasters.
story: Update: Isaias became a hurricane late Wednesday night. See the latest forecast here.
Tropical Storm Isaias was "quickly intensifying" and is expected to approach the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday after becoming a hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center.

Currently swirling in the Gulf, Isaias would be the Atlantic basin's first hurricane of the season and is its ninth named storm. An El Niño climate pattern continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The storm formed with less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, which ends Nov. 30.
Maps show possible path

Tropical Storm Isaias, which grew from Tropical Depression Nine on Wednesday and is pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," is expected to pass to the north of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday and make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast of the U.S. late Friday or early Saturday, the hurricane center said.

A hurricane warning was issued Wednesday for the northern Gulf Coast, from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Florida's Bay/Gulf county line, and a tropical storm warning was issued from Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to Ocean Springs, and from the Bay/Gulf county line to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge warning was also issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida, according to the hurricane center.

Tropical storm-force winds were extending outward up to 60 miles from the storm's center on Wednesday evening. Its maximum sustained winds were 70 mph, and it was forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday morning, the hurricane center said.
A storm's maximum wind speed must rise to at least 74 mph to be considered a hurricane.

Isaias is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places on the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see rainfall ranging from 1 to 5 inches, forecasters said.
Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.

The hurricane center on Thursday warned of "an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts" along parts of the northern Gulf Coast and urged people living in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi and northern Florida to "closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place."

At high tide, the approximately 300-mile stretch between Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and Indian Pass, Florida, could see a storm surge of up to 7 feet, forecasters said, potentially causing major flooding.
In addition to rain, the hurricane center said Isaias could potentially bring urban flooding and isolated river flooding to places in its path.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."
On Wednesday, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a similar state of emergency for 40 counties, saying in a statement that it will allow Alabama officials "to take any needed steps ahead of landfall."
Beware the "I"-named storm
While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.
The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017) and Irene (2011).
When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

title: Texas executes man after lawyers sought to stop procedure, citing Christa Pike
summary: Jamaal Howard was executed by lethal injection after his lawyers tried to argue that he faced risks similar to Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's attempt to put her to death.
story: A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee's failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike.

Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. local time after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was convicted of killing Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery caught on surveillance video.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to members of his victim's family who watched through a window a few feet from him.

Earlier Wednesday, Howard's attorneys unsuccessfully sought to block the execution by arguing that he was intellectually disabled and faced risks similar to those in Pike's case because both states use pentobarbital for lethal injections.

The court denied the request for a stay and later denied a second attempt to stop Howard's execution over the drug. The court issued both denials without elaboration. The U.S. Supreme Court also denied a late appeal Wednesday evening without comment.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys argued in their filing.

Pike's lawyers were seeking more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. She was hospitalized and, as of Tuesday, had regained consciousness and was speaking, her lawyers said, but she is unable to move her arms or hands.

Pike's attorneys have alleged her execution was marred by blown veins, where a needle goes all the way through a vein and causes a leak of blood and fluid, as well as Tennessee's deteriorated pentobarbital and a lack of emergency medical care.

"There is a similar risk," Howard's attorneys wrote, "that Texas's execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind."
Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard, who became the 30th execution nationwide in 2026.
Inmate remained "chatty" on drive to the death chamber

On Wednesday, Howard was described as "chatty" during the 45-mile drive from the death row prison to the Huntsville Unit where executions are carried out, said Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.
"He made small talk with the officers through the whole trip," she said, adding he was taken to a small holding cell near the death chamber, where he remained talkative.
"He was asking questions and was very engaged in the process," Hernandez said.
A killing caught on surveillance video

Howard was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest during a robbery. Evidence presented at the trial included the store's surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles northeast of Houston, according to court records.

His attorneys have argued that Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities.
Motion to stay because of drugs

The motion filed in the Court of Criminal Appeals in Texas early Wednesday said Howard's attorneys had filed requests for information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use. They say the department asked for a state attorney general opinion about whether they would have to disclose that information, despite a "years-long practice of disclosing information."
Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday morning.
Executions in the U.S. this year
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.
Tennessee's Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.

An execution date for former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, has been set for Dec. 3, and will take place at the same post where he carried out his attack, according to an email sent to the families of victims.

Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.

title: Protesters ejected from raucous Trump rally in Texas
summary: Several hecklers were removed from President Trump's rally in Texas late Wednesday, drawing jeers from the crowd as the president made fun of the protesters.
story: Several hecklers were removed from President Trump's rally in Texas late Wednesday.

At least 10 people were either ejected from the venue by authorities or appeared to walk out after interrupting the rally, drawing jeers from the crowd at San Antonio's Freeman Coliseum as Mr. Trump mocked the protesters. It's the president's third trip to Texas in recent weeks to support Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who is facing a tougher-than-expected contest against Democratic candidate James Talarico.

Less than 10 minutes into Mr. Trump's speech, a person stormed away from the stage while yelling. At one point, a man in a red hat grabbed that person's hair and appeared to get into a physical altercation, leading other rallygoers to separate the two. After the person walked out of the venue, the president asked: "Is there anything like a Trump rally?"
"He's going back home to mom right now," the president said. "What he doesn't know is that his mom voted for Trump."

For the next hour, several other people were walked out of the venue by law enforcement or security while the crowd booed them. In some cases, Trump supporters and demonstrators were separated after physically tangling with each other.
At least one person was handcuffed before law enforcement led him out.
The president poked fun at several of the attendees who were ejected, saying one person has "got to lose a lot of weight" and others were "really bad-looking people."
CBS News has reached out to local authorities and the U.S. Secret Service for more information on the ejections.

Mr. Trump was on stage for well over an hour. He spent much of the event railing against Talarico, a state lawmaker who is aiming to be the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. Most polls show Talarico either with a narrow edge or neck-and-neck with Paxton, a state attorney general with a polarizing record who frustrated other Republicans by ousting Sen. John Cornyn in a primary earlier this year.

Republicans have sought to cast Talarico as too liberal for Texas, a theme that Mr. Trump emphasized throughout the evening, jabbing Talarico for his record in the state legislature. The president said if Talarico wins, he would turn Texas into a "dirty, failing, crime-ridden third-world dumping ground."

Mr. Trump also spent a large amount of time on immigration, touting the precipitous drop in unauthorized border crossings in recent years. The issue dominated Mr. Trump's 2024 campaign but has become more challenging for him as most voters grow skeptical of his administration's hardline enforcement tactics — particularly Hispanic voters, whose shift toward Mr. Trump helped propel him to victory in 2024.

title: 1 dead, 3 missing after boat sinks near Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay
summary: One person died and three were missing in San Francisco Bay on Tuesday after a boat with 20 people on board sank near Alcatraz Island, authorities said.
story: As of July 27, a single passenger remains missing from the Volare.
One person died and three were missing in the San Francisco Bay on Tuesday after a boat with 20 people on board sank near Alcatraz Island, authorities said.
The San Francisco Fire Department and the U.S. Coast Guard responded to a call at about 3:30 p.m. of a boat fire between the Golden Gate Bridge and Alcatraz.

San Francisco Fire Chief Dean Crispen said a police marine unit arrived first and saw a man in the water in "severe distress" and brought him onto their boat, where they began CPR. He was then taken to Gashouse Cove, where he was declared dead.
Crispen said 19 people were initially believed to be on the boat, but witness accounts put the number at 20.

Thirteen passengers were brought safely to shore, while three were taken to a hospital and were in stable condition. Crispen said most of their injuries were impact injuries from jumping into the water.
Three people remain missing, the fire chief said.

San Francisco Fire Lt. Mariano Elias said the boat, named Volare, was based out of Stockton and was a 50-foot cabin cruiser. It was not immediately clear what caused the boat to sink about 600 yards from Alcatraz.

"The information we have is that it left from St. Francis Yacht Club, and the initial report was a vessel on fire. Upon arrival, our members did not evidence any fire. The reports we've had from witnesses is that there was rough seas and apparently the vessel began to take on water and was turned over in the bay," Crispen said.
Crews had 11 vessels involved in the effort to find the missing boaters, Crispen said, and they planned to continue their search through the night.

"I want to make sure that every family member out there and everybody knows that we are in an active search," San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said. "This is an all-hands-on-deck search and, hopefully, rescue."
Crispen said all the people on board are adults, and most of them are family members.
"Our understanding was there was some sort of memorial service they were engaging in. That's why they were using this particular vessel," Crispen said.
Officials set up a family reunification center at Fort Mason, which is west of Fisherman's Wharf, and the 13 taken safely to shore were at the center.
Crispen said the initial rescue also involved the Oakland Police Department's marine unit and private vessels in addition to the Coast Guard.
Anyone who believes a family member may have been on the boat and is looking for more information should call 1-800-RED CROSS (800-733-2767).

title: Alleged Chinese agent to remain in custody, judge rules, amid flight-risk fears
summary: California realtor Wanying Zhang is facing federal prosecution for allegedly surveilling the Taiwanese president's son in Washington last year at the direction of Chinese government officials.
story: An alleged Chinese agent arrested at Los Angeles International Airport over the weekend will remain in federal custody, a federal judge ruled Wednesday during a court hearing. The decision comes amid concern from the FBI that she may try to flee the country if released, law enforcement sources previously told CBS News.
Prosecutors successfully argued that 34-year-old realtor Wanying Zhang posed too great a flight risk. She had offered to post more than $1.2 million in property for her bond.
Prosecutors told Judge Steve Kim at the L.A. hearing that Zhang has a brother with a history of working for the Chinese government, and that her parents and siblings live in China.
The Orange County mother is now facing federal prosecution for allegedly surveilling the Taiwanese president's son in Washington last year at the direction of Chinese government officials.
Investigators have said Zhang owned a business in China, regularly has money deposited in a Chinese bank account and has parents, a brother and sister currently living there, CBS News has learned.
One law enforcement source said Zhang also had a Chinese passport that was not recovered during an FBI search of her home. Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Elbogen confirmed this Wednesday in court.
The sources provided information anonymously as they were not authorized to speak on the record. Zhang's husband and sister declined to comment.

Elbogen told the court Wednesday that Zhang had received $190,000 into a Chinese bank account from an "unregistered cryptocurrency exchange" business and had "hundreds of thousands of dollars" at her disposal in China.
Zhang is currently in the custody of U.S. Marshals in Los Angeles. She was arrested Sunday trying to board a flight to Shanghai at LAX, CBS News was first to report.

She previously appeared briefly in court on Monday, represented by a public defender. The judge had told Zhang to get a private defense attorney by the time of her detention hearing Wednesday, which she did.
Prosecutors Wednesday accused Zhang of lying on the forms she filled out declaring her assets after her arrest, saying that she only had one property when in fact she had several.
Zhang's defense attorney, Craig Harbaugh, told the judge it was a "misunderstanding."
However, Kim noted "inconsistencies" about the number of properties and assets Zhang owns and "where the money is coming from."
During the hearing, Elbogen also referred to Zhang as a "secret agent of a hostile foreign power" and accused her of "spying" on behalf of the Chinese government.

"She has been lying to her own family about who she is," Elbogen told the court. Elbogen claimed Zhang has traveled to China 12 times since 2014 and internationally 29 times, including to Paris, France and Japan.

Harbaugh countered that the only allegation the government has made of spying dated back to September 2025, and that his client's last contact with her Chinese government handlers, according to the complaint, was in October 2025.

Zhang appeared in court Wednesday in shackles and a white jumpsuit. Her husband, Eric Ding, a realtor at the same Irvine, California, firm as his wife, watched from the public gallery with his sister, attorney Elaine Lori, beside him. Both Ding and Lori attended Monday's hearing as well.

According to the criminal complaint against Zhang, she attended the University of International Relations in Beijing between 2010 and 2014, which is run by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's intelligence agency and secret police.
FBI counterintelligence special agent Kevin Holt wrote in his affidavit in the complaint that the ministry "recruits heavily" from the university.
Two law enforcement sources told CBS News that Zhang was one of the top students in her class at UIR.
Zhang's Facebook page shows she is friends with eight current or former staff and students at the university.

As an example of Zhang's alleged Chinese government connections, Elbogen said Wednesday that when Zhang lived in China, she was able to fast-track government permission to move her residence from Beijing to another city.

In its criminal complaint, the FBI said it obtained Zhang's text messages with Chinese intelligence officials, plotting and executing a plan last year to secretly film Taiwan's first son, Lai Ting-yu, and his family in the Seattle suburb where they live. Investigators alleged they have footage from a neighbor's security camera catching Zhang in the midst of her alleged surveillance mission.

Zhang's suspected accomplice on her alleged Seattle trip, named only as Individual 1 in the complaint, left on a one-way ticket to China about two weeks ago, prosecutors said during Wednesday's hearing.
On Tuesday, CBS News also revealed Zhang's links to a Chinese American advocacy group with deep ties to the Chinese government.

She traveled to San Francisco with the organization, the All American Chinese Association, to celebrate Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit there in 2023. Pro-China activists then attacked pro-democracy protesters outside Xi's hotel. There is no evidence Zhang was involved in the violence.

A photograph shows her behind an AACA banner, standing next to the group's leader, Edward Cai, who previously served as vice president for an organization so close to the Chinese government, it was forced to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
FARA requires agents of foreign governments to inform the Justice Department of their status and any lobbying, attempted influence or other activities in the U.S.
Cai and the AACA did not respond to a request for comment.
Reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet." He declined to comment further on Monday in federal court.

title: Christa Pike has pneumonia, unable to move arms after botched execution
summary: Attorneys for Christa Pike, the Tennessee inmate who survived two doses of a lethal injection during her botched execution last week, shared an update on her health condition.
story: Christa Pike's attorneys said she has pneumonia, a blood clot, couldn't swallow, and is unable to move her arms or hands once she regained consciousness in a Tennessee hospital, days after the death row inmate survived a botched execution by the state.
"Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove," said one of Pike's attorneys, Randy Spivey, at a Wednesday news conference. "It was extraordinary."
Spivey said he and Pike's other attorneys were told she was brain-dead on Monday and expected her to be removed from life support. But by the next day, she had woken up and started talking, he said.
The attorney said it was his understanding that Pike's first words were, "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"

"I don't have an explanation for what happened," Spivey told reporters after a hearing at Davidson County Chancery Court. He said that Pike was confused and disoriented at first, but she began to remember details of the execution attempt on Wednesday.

In addition to the lung infection, a blood clot in her arm, and an issue swallowing that had prevented her from eating, Pike's arms and hands are "tremendously swollen," said Spivey, adding that "we don't know what function she will regain."
Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S., according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Court grants request for evidence

Before Pike's attorneys shared updates on her health outside of the Davidson County court on Wednesday, they attended an emergency hearing in which they requested Tennessee's correctional department to preserve records and other evidence of her failed lethal injection.

Chancellor I'Ashea Myles granted the order and said the state would be mandated to preserve "relevant evidence" of its failed attempt to put Pike to death on Sept. 30, including "drugs, IV lines, needles, catheters, medical supplies, restraints, gurneys" and anything else in the execution chamber at the time of the procedure.

Myles said waste, such as packing supplies and labels, and all written or digital records, including records of communication through encrypted platforms, witness accounts, and correspondence regarding equipment or drug administration issues, must be preserved, too.
She explicitly directed the state "not to lose, misplace, accidentally delete, any information that may be pertinent to this litigation."

"To any extent that any information or any evidence has already been discarded, deleted, destroyed or no longer exists, I want [the Tennessee Department of Correction] to take an affirmative step to try to claw back that information and put in policies and procedures, while this incident litigation is pending, to ensure that no information is discarded or destroyed," said Myles.
Execution aftermath

Staff had given Pike, 50, two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. Her legal team said on Tuesday that she had regained consciousness and was speaking from her hospital bed.

Pike's attorneys also said Tuesday she was continuing "to receive critical medical care" as hospital workers attempted to clear her system of the lethal drug pentobarbital. Her prognosis remained unclear, they added, but she was expected to face, at minimum, "a long recovery."

The legal team has renewed its calls for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's death sentence, pushing him to change the sentence to life in prison without parole so that the state can't attempt to execute Pike a second time, which is the usual course of action after an inmate survives botched execution proceedings. However, while others have survived botched procedures before, Pike is the only known inmate in the United States' modern death penalty era to remain alive after actually receiving lethal chemicals.

"The state has made no promises that Ms. Pike will not be subject to a future execution," Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's attorneys, said in court on Wednesday. Evidence sought by the defense for the correctional department to preserve could help them build future arguments to prevent that from happening, Ihnen added.
Will Ayers, the assistant attorney general for the state of Tennessee, told the court that there's no pending execution order for Pike, and "there is no allegation that one is coming."

Attorneys for Pike had filed an emergency motion Friday asking that the correctional department be required to "preserve all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence" of the failed execution, which, they said, amounted to "evidence of TDOC [Tennessee Department of Correction] inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol."

They accused correctional staff tasked with handling Pike's execution of failing to properly establish an IV line through which to administer lethal drugs, and then failing to realize she had a "blown vein," allegedly allowing pentobarbital to spread through her body and causing a painful, botched procedure. In court, Ihnen also referenced the secrecy that shrouds execution protocols and proceedings in Tennessee and elsewhere across the U.S., which makes arguing death penalty cases particularly challenging.
"We don't know what they have, because they won't tell us," Ihnen said in court. "And so the preservation order seeks the broadest possible preservation of evidence."
Case history

Lee had denied Pike's request for a commuted sentence before her execution date last week, rejecting her clemency petition in the days leading up to it. In its aftermath, he canceled the one remaining execution scheduled to take place in Tennessee by the end of the year and said an investigation would be conducted to determine what went wrong. The now-former Tennessee correctional commissioner stepped down from his post, although an official statement from the agency claimed it had followed protocols.

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the killing and spent more than three decades on Tennessee's death row. As the only woman awaiting execution in the state for a vast majority of that time, she was alone for almost the entirety of her incarceration. She was the first woman Tennessee attempted to execute in more than 200 years and the first person the state attempted to execute in modern times for a crime they committed at age 18, 19 or 20.

Prior to Pike's botched injection, her case had garnered public interest as human rights leaders and advocacy groups rallied against her death sentence, raising issues with her age at the time of her conviction and long history of mental illness and childhood abuse. But those who strongly support her execution, including prosecutors and jurors in Pike's original trial as well as judges who presided over that case and many of her appeals, have countered that capital punishment is warranted given the horrific nature of her crime. Among them is Slemmer's mother, May Martinez.

title: Maduro expected to face new charges of torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons
summary: An attorney for Maduro told CBS News that he has not been given notice that additional charges could be coming.
story: Federal prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, for allegedly torturing Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to multiple sources familiar with the case.

The sources said that additional people could be charged in their role for the torture of more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government while Maduro was in power.
One source said the new charges could be announced as soon as Thursday.
Barry Pollack, an attorney for Maduro, told CBS News that he has not been provided any notice that additional charges could be coming.
Flores is due in federal court on Thursday in the Southern District of New York for a bond hearing, and a trial date has been tentatively set for June 2027.
CNN was first to report the potential new charges.
A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government. The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty.
Prosecutors said Maduro was at the "forefront of the corruption" and that he and his associates worked with drug traffickers and narco-terrorists to flood the U.S. with drugs.

Maduro faces four charges: narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
The case against them was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.

Maduro and his wife have asked U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leaders of a foreign country. The judge has not heard arguments on those motions yet.

In September, Alex Saab, a former minister of industry in Maduro's government, pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering tied to an alleged bribery conspiracy and agreed to cooperate in ongoing federal investigations into the regime after being deported to the U.S. from Venezuela.
In May, CBS News reported that federal prosecutors in Miami were ordered to open a new criminal investigation into Maduro amid some concerns that the pending prosecution against him is weak.

title: Trump pitches Trump International Golf Course for site of "presidential retreat"
summary: It's not yet clear what the taxpayer benefit would be for such a build, or how much it would cost.
story: Washington — President Trump on Wednesday claimed the U.S. Secret Service and U.S. military suggested developing Trump International Golf Course in West Palm Beach as a presidential getaway. It would be "like sort of a Camp David retreat" for future presidents, Mr. Trump said.

"This was suggested to me by the military and Secret Service," the president said during an unrelated event in the Oval Office. "There are no high buildings looming over it. There are no houses on it so you don't have houses — we have to inspect rooms. Seems that all presidents play golf."

A White House official said Wednesday that the "United States government has asked to look into developing a presidential retreat" at the golf course so future presidents can "hold important meetings and utilize the amenities of a world-class property."

Trump International Golf Course is where Mr. Trump plays golf when he's staying at his resort at Mar-a-Lago. The Palm Beach Post first reported that an attorney for the golf course wrote a letter to Palm Beach County commissioners offering to designate the golf club as a presidential retreat that could also be used by foreign heads of state.

"The United States government has asked to look into developing a presidential retreat at Trump International Golf Course in Palm Beach for future presidents, so they can hold important meetings and utilize the amenities of a world-class property," the White House official said. "The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly-rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat."
The White House official's statement did not specify whose idea the retreat was first, or whose permission they're seeking.
The cost of the proposed development — and who would bear it — has not been disclosed.
In December, the president is hosting the G20 summit of world leaders at a different property, Trump National Doral Miami.
The Secret Service has paid the Trump Organization hundreds of thousands of dollars to stay at the president's properties during his presidency.

title: Union alleges Bureau of Prisons in contempt for failing to reinstate collective bargaining agreement
summary: Last week, a judge in Connecticut blocked the Bureau of Prisons from terminating its collective bargaining agreement.
story: The union representing 30,000 Bureau of Prisons employees is asking a federal judge to hold the agency in contempt, alleging that prison leadership has refused to follow the court's order to immediately restore its collective bargaining agreement.

The contempt request, filed Oct. 6, comes just one week after U.S. District Judge Vernon Oliver in Connecticut granted a motion for a preliminary injunction against the Bureau of Prisons that was sought by the National Council of Prison Locals.

Bureau of Prisons Director William Marshall terminated the collective bargaining agreement on Sept. 25, 2025. He alleged the union posed an "obstacle to progress" and said it was not the "kind of union" he could support.

The judge ruled that the union was likely to succeed on the merits of its argument that the BOP had violated the Administrative Procedure Act by terminating the collective bargaining agreement and ordered the bureau to reinstate it immediately.

In its motion for contempt, the union alleged that bureau leadership is stonewalling and refusing to allow the union to resume its usual operations, including by allowing people to have "official" union time.
In one such example, the motion and an accompanying sworn statement said that a BOP employee who was facing termination asked to be represented by a shop steward at the meeting.
"There ain't no union," a BOP official allegedly told the employee, according to the motion. The employee was terminated on Oct. 5.

In another allegation, the union said that Marshall told people on Sept. 29, hours before the court ruling hit the docket, that he had no plans to enforce the terms of the collective bargaining agreement unless he received direct orders from the White House.

"They have not restored union office space or official time, allowed for union representation in disciplinary proceedings, or taken any of the other myriad specific steps that Defendants themselves told the court would be required if the court entered the requested injunction," attorneys for the union wrote.
"Defendants' noncompliance is total."

In a press release issued by American Federation of Government Employees Local 1237, which represents employees at FCI Mendota, the union alleged that management in that facility had also locked union officials out of their offices.
The Bureau of Prisons declined to comment, citing the pending litigation.
Since the court's original Sept. 29 order granting the union's request for a preliminary injunction, the Justice Department has not formally sought a stay to pause the ruling.
On Oct. 2, however, the Justice Department filed a formal "notice of compliance" with the court. In that filing, it said BOP was "aware" of the court's order and "complying with its terms."

But at the same time, the department also said that it did not understand the court's ruling to mean that the BOP could not proceed with trying to re-terminate the collective bargaining agreement again before it expires in May 2028.
It also added that the Justice Department did not expect the U.S. District Court would be supervising "every alleged failure" by BOP to comply with the collective bargaining agreement.
The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate unions at multiple federal agencies.

In March 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that sought to exclude federal offices involved in national security or intelligence work from having collective bargaining agreements with staff. That order also applied to the Justice Department, which includes the Bureau of Prisons.
But after the order was made public, the BOP allowed its union to continue operating for approximately six months before terminating the collective bargaining agreement.
In doing so, Marshall at the time did not cite national security as a basis for his decision.

title: "America's Startup" competitors use AI to launch businesses from their dorms
summary: Young entrepreneurs are tapping AI to launch a range of businesses, from analyzing your skin to helping wine growers analyze crop yields.
story: One startup uses artificial intelligence to help winemakers better predict crop yields. Another uses insights gleaned from AI to enable earlier detection of skin cancer, while a third develops a seaweed-based hydrogel fire suppressant that's free of "forever chemicals."

The entrepreneurs behind these tech-forward startups have one thing in common: They started the companies from their college dorm rooms to participate in "America's Startup," a government-backed collegiate innovation competition that's part of America250, the congressional commission behind the U.S.'s 250th anniversary celebration.

America250 chair and the 43rd Treasurer of the U.S., Rosie Rios, who leads America's Startup, told CBS News she expects a wave of innovation led by Generation Z entrepreneurs, who will be the first AI-native cohort of workers to enter the job market upon graduation.

"They really hit the ground running and are not intimidated by it," Rios said. She also thinks AI will help broaden the skills and experience of new entrants to the job market, much as the internet did for millennials.
"It's no longer what they learned at home or in a classroom — it's what they see and have access to," said Rios, adding that AI helps eliminate some of the hurdles to launching companies.
"Idea machines"

Recent research from the Bank of America Institute shows the rate of U.S. business formation is rising, largely driven by Gen Z founders. In June, Gen Z surpassed all other generations in growth in new business registration applications. Researchers concluded that starting a business may be viewed as a desirable pathway to career success as younger workers navigate a challenging labor market.

Additionally, AI can be deployed to perform functions such as bookkeeping or content creation, allowing founders to operate as "solopreneurs" and save on personnel costs, researchers at the Bank of America Institute noted.

"They've been exposed to so much because of their comfort with technology that they are basically idea machines," Rios told CBS News. "AI could be very advantageous for this group, and they have demonstrated their ability to use it for good, so far."

Kayan Shah, a college sophomore and co-founder of Graft Systems, was one of 10 winners of last year's America's Startup competition. He's partnering with vineyards across San Francisco to test and further develop the company's technology, which collects images of plants and combines them with machine-learning models that predict how many grapes they'll yield by analyzing variables such as weather, sunlight and a vineyard's location.
"AI could take over many, many jobs, but this is the status quo, so the only option you have is to make the best of it, and we're using it to help wine growers," Shah said.

While Shah isn't yet 21 and can't legally drink, he said he appreciates wine culture and wants to preserve it, citing a decline in alcohol consumption rates. Americans who say they drink alcohol fell to 54% last year, the lowest level in 90 years, according to an August 2025 Gallup poll.
Skin in the game

Another entrant in last year's startup contest pitched a biotech company that helps people track their exposure to harmful ultraviolet rays and potentially detect skin cancer earlier. Kristina Schiffman, the founder of UV Sense, told CBS News the company uses AI to educate people about their skin, including a tool for analyzing and tracking moles and other conditions.
"We take user inputs, including images and concerns about the skin, and use AI to help people make an informed decision about what they should do," Schiffman said.
"If you have a freckle you're concerned about, you can upload photos and use AI to monitor its shape, size and color, and we can recommend a dermatologist visit," she explained.

Aspiring entrepreneurs can submit their best ideas to America's Startup before applications close on Oct. 8 at 7:59 p.m. EDT. The competition will award a total of $1 million in cash and prizes to a series of winners. Applicant teams can win up to $50,000 each.

An investor council, which will review proposals and have the opportunity to invest, includes some of the nation's most prominent entrepreneurs, such as Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak and Sarah Friar, chief financial officer at ChatGPT developer OpenAI.

title: Congress tried to stop surprise medical bills. It created another problem.
summary: Healthcare providers and middlemen are exploiting a loophole in a 2020 law designed to shield consumers from surprise medical bills.
story: A law designed to protect patients from surprise medical bills succeeded in eliminating unexpected charges, but spawned a lucrative arbitration industry with providers and specialized middlemen extracting payments far above benchmark billing rates.
The practice is ultimately driving up healthcare costs for consumers, a CBS News investigation found.

The arbitration system Congress created to settle disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers allows doctors and resolution specialists acting on their behalf to win payments many times higher than typical rates for medical services. Those costs don't disappear: Much of the money comes from employer-sponsored health plans, meaning workers may ultimately pay through higher premiums or reduced benefits.

Under the arbitration system established by the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, insurers are paying healthcare providers hundreds of dollars for routine lab tests that typically cost between $10 and $30, industry researchers told CBS News. In one instance, a plastic surgeon was awarded more than $400,000 to perform a breast reduction, a procedure the insurer said it had previously paid the doctor between $6,000 and $30,000 to perform.
The plastic surgeon, Dr. Norman Rowe, routinely was awarded around 170 times the benchmark rates for his services under the NSA's arbitration system, a CBS News analysis of public data shows.
A spokesman for Dr. Rowe told CBS News that insurers had manipulated benchmark rates to lowball doctors and create "artificially low reimbursement rates."

"Dr. Rowe uses the widely recognized gold standard FairHealth benchmarks set by the independent nonprofit FairHealth.org using reliable and objective market data. FairHealth data is so reliable that it is incorporated into statutes and regulations around the country and serves as the official data source for many state health programs," the spokesman added.

In addition to the typical benchmark rate arbitrators consider (known as the "qualifying payment amount," or QPA), FairHealth provides another rate that can be used during the dispute resolution process. Medicare rates, meanwhile, may not be considered.

CBS News found that another doctor — Long Island spine surgeon Vadim Lerman — was being awarded an average of 280 times the benchmark rates in arbitration. He declined an interview, but a spokesman for Lerman said that "the suggestion that a physician is receiving 'hundreds of times' above benchmark rates is incorrect. No comparison should be made to the insurer's initial offer — which can be inappropriately low for a complex surgical procedure — and the award given to the physician."
"Baseball-style arbitration"
Insurers have, in many cases, been forced to pay high rates like those Dr. Rowe charges under the law's so-called "baseball-style" or "pendulum" arbitration system.

In an arbitration under the No Surprises Act, insurers and providers each propose a rate for a given service. There's no room for negotiation, as an arbitrator must choose between one of the two parties' suggested figures.

Arbitrators side with providers in more than 85% of the cases, according to Leland Robbins, a product leader at Turquoise Health, a data transparency startup. Some arbitrators – officially called certified Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR, entities – have track records of siding with providers in an even larger share of cases, according to Robbins' group.
He told CBS News that while patients are no longer being surprised by large medical bills, there is a catch to the new system.

"The transaction didn't go away. It went behind closed doors and has moved into this arbitration process when a payer and a provider can't agree what the fair price should be," Robbins said. "Given that 70% of these awards are being taken out of employer-sponsored health plans, consumers are going to start seeing it when it comes time for open enrollment."
He added, "You know, employers are not able to withstand and absorb these kinds of big fees. They're going to be probably not paying for as much of your premiums."

Last year, 15 government-certified arbitrators earned fees per case, with 17 arbitrators designated to do this work today. Each side in the dispute — the healthcare provider and the insurer — pays into the process prior to the arbitrator making any decision.

During the first six months of 2025, insurers and providers submitted 1.2 million new disputes to the arbitration portal, while federal officials had only expected approximately 17,000 cases per year, research from the Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR) at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy shows.
However, HaloMD, a company that files cases on behalf of providers, told CBS News that the initial estimates "were objectively flawed in how they calculated expected volume."
Collectively, arbitrators making the decisions have earned more than $2 billion in fees. None agreed to on-camera interviews with CBS News.
New Jersey House Rep. Frank Pallone, a Democrat and the lead sponsor of the No Surprises Act, blames private equity, in part, for breaking the system he helped create.
He said just a few private equity firms – which are increasingly buying up anesthesiology, radiology and emergency room practices — are driving arbitration cases.

Pallone told CBS News that doctors should be paid the equivalent of in-network rates for the services they provide, but said "we had no choice" but to introduce the arbitration system "if we wanted to actually get rid of surprise billing."
"I knew it was not going to go well, but I didn't know it was going to be this bad," he added.
Dispute resolution cottage industry

The law's arbitration provision has also created an opportunity for intermediaries to guide providers through the process and rake in profits by taking a cut of bills that are up to 1,000% above the benchmark rate for a service, CBS News found. Critics argue that such firms demand more money on providers' behalf, leading to the large settlements that drive up everyone's costs.

HaloMD bills itself as "the expert" in arbitration cases brought under the No Surprises Act. Founded by Texas couple Scott and Alla Laroque in 2022, the same year the No Surprises Act took effect, the company is one of the fledgling industry's biggest players.

Private equity firms also sometimes own both physician staffing firms and Independent Dispute Resolution entities, creating a conflict of interest and undermining the law's fairness. HaloMD is not private equity-backed, but Halo and two other groups with investments from buyout firms collectively handled more than 75% of disputes settled in arbitration last year, according to Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms.

According to Halo, the firm made more than $1 billion for its clients, routinely earning awards that are nine times the benchmark rates for services. Halo takes a cut of the payouts but has not disclosed the amount.

Halo chief external affairs officer Patrick Velliky told CBS News that insurance companies, not firms like his, are responsible for driving up consumer healthcare costs by either not participating in the arbitration process or submitting ludicrously low offers.

"24% of the time, insurers lose by default. They didn't submit an offer at all. Another 9 1/2% of the time, insurers submit an offer, like a dollar or less," Velliky told CBS News. "So what that actually looks like, a patient goes to the E-D with a heart attack, we go to arbitration and the insurer is offering a total of $1.00."

He also said that insurance companies are offering misleading information about the benchmark rate. "Whatever the actual median in-network rate is, it's not what the insurer presented," Velliky told CBS News. "They're miscalculating it."
A federal court sided with providers on the issue this summer, saying the benchmark rate is "artificially low," pulled down by insurers' $0- or $ 1-reimbursement offers to doctors.
Proposed reforms
Pallone wants to reform the law to gut what he sees as the root of the issues arising from the No Surprises Act: arbitration.

He plans to introduce legislation this week to eliminate the arbitration process and stipulate that providers be paid in-network rates, even if they are out-of-network. Pallone's office also told CBS News that so-called ghost rates, which often drag the benchmark rate down, will be excluded from calculations moving forward.

"Whether it's the hospitals, the doctors, the nurse, they're really trying to care for people. Of course, all of them should have a decent income so they can live," the New Jersey lawmaker said. "But why should these outside investors be making all this money off the backs of, you know, your insurance premiums, essentially?"

title: Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power" in Acropolis speech
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
story: Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.

In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.

"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.

"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."

His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.

The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.

In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."

"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.

"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."

The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.

The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.

Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."

In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.

Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.

"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.

The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.

"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.

In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.

The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."

title: Why you just got a $90 Social Security check — and who missed out
summary: Millions of seniors are getting $90 direct deposits from Social Security this week, prompting questions about the source of the money.
story: Millions of seniors are receiving $90 deposits from the Social Security Administration this week, prompting some to question the source of the money. The checks are tied to the Trump administration's announcement that it would send checks to about 20 million Medicare enrollees to lower healthcare costs.

President Trump on Friday announced that the administration would send the money to some participants in the healthcare plan's Part B, which pays for doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings. About one-third of Medicare Part B's 62.9 million enrollees are eligible, with about 40 million not qualifying for the payments.

The payments are funded by the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress to improve and support the original Medicare fee-for-service program. Experts say the $90, while helpful, won't fully offset higher costs facing Medicare recipients.

Premiums for Part B rose by more than $200 annually in 2026 and are projected to increase by nearly $80 in 2027, according to the Medicare trustees' most recent annual report. The standard monthly premium for Part B in 2026 is $202.90, a figure that's expected to rise to $209.50 next year.
Americans of all ages are grappling with rising healthcare costs, which they cite as a top financial concern, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.
Who qualifies for the $90 checks?

Seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare and who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid are eligible for the one-time payment. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage are ineligible for the payments.
That leaves more than 20 million Part B enrollees who are eligible, according to a CMS fact sheet.

"People who are paying the income-related premium have higher incomes to begin with, so the thinking is that they may be better able to absorb higher costs and wouldn't benefit as much from the $90 payment as people with lower incomes," Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, told CBS News.
Medicare Advantage isn't the same as traditional Medicare, which is likely why those enrollees don't qualify for the payments, she added.
The agency said the initiative improves Medicare and makes coverage more affordable by putting "healthcare dollars back where they belong – in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries."
How will the money be sent?

Most eligible beneficiaries will receive the $90 rebate through a direct deposit from the Social Security Administration on or around Oct. 8, according to the CMS fact sheet. Some seniors reported receiving the payments or pending deposits on Tuesday, according to social media reports.

Some beneficiaries will receive a $90 paper check from the U.S. Department of the Treasury later in October. It will include the following message: "Medicare Improvement Fund Payment; $90 Payment to Offset October Premium."
Some advocates say the paper payments could go unnoticed by seniors, especially given the volume of mail many receive from insurers during open enrollment season.
Why are 40 million people left out?
About 40 million Medicare Part B enrollees are ineligible for the $90 payment. They include:
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plansThose who pay an income-related adjusted premiumPeople who do not live in the U.S.Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans
Those who pay an income-related adjusted premium
People who do not live in the U.S.
Beneficiaries who receive premium assistance

Eligible beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Part B can call 1-800-MEDICARE to determine whether or not they qualify for the one-time check. Beneficiaries who want to check on the status of their payment can call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213 beginning on Oct. 15.

title: Americans are paying 62% more for water than a decade ago, study finds
summary: Americans paid an average of $531 per year for household water in 2025, although people in some states pay far more, according to a new study.
story: Americans aren't only paying more for food amid stubbornly high inflation — the cost of washing it down has also surged.

Water costs have shot up across the U.S., with a new study by the nonprofit advocacy group Food and Water Watch showing that households are paying 62% more for water at home than a decade ago. Those expenses are rising as utilities invest more in aging infrastructure and in adapting their systems to cope with the effects of climate change, Food and Water Watch said in its study.

Federal support for the nation's water infrastructure has declined. The 2025 Infrastructure Report Card, an evaluation by the American Society of Civil Engineers, said that since fiscal year 2022, Congress has appropriated at least $1 billion below the authorized funding levels for a federal fund that supports state water infrastructure projects.

A 2023 survey by the Environmental Protection Agency projects that drinking water systems across the U.S. will need $625 billion in investment over the next two years to implement upgrades and meet health requirements.

Food and Water Watch based its findings on data from 500 of the largest community water systems around the country that serve a combined 155 million people. More specifically, Food and Water Watch looked at how much utilities charged for 60,000 gallons of water, the estimated amount households use for drinking, showering, laundry and similar purposes in a year. The study did not include bills for wastewater or stormwater, which are managed by separate utilities.
How are water costs changing across the country?

The average water bill across the 500 systems Food and Water Watch studied was $531 last year. However, the amount someone pays can vary widely depending on where they live. The government-run water system in Hempstead, New York, charged people an average of $133 a year last year, the lowest rate of the systems examined in the study.
On the other end of the spectrum is San Jose, California, where the private-sector company San Jose Water charged residents an average of $1,416 in 2025, up 163% from a decade ago, the group found.

The state with the lowest overall bills was Idaho, where three of its largest water systems charged an average of $286 in 2025. West Virginia, which has some of the highest poverty rates in the country, had the highest bills. The two largest systems there, owned by American Water, charged an average of $1,383 a year, according to Food and Water Watch.

Costs were higher in counties where water systems are run by for-profit corporations, the group said. Those private companies charged an average of $823 for water in 2025, $329 more than what the public systems charged.
